bullets: Unreachable Oracles introduces an offline audit for checking whether each benchmark answer can actually be derived from the information an agent receives. Its rule traces both the target value and every construction step through a declared, finite set of permitted derivations. QAMQOR and radarvitals-audit expose the related problem of test leakage through shared participants: scores can reflect recognition of a child, session, or subject rather than the intended capability. Together, these releases make benchmark validity a recurring design pressure in this captured feed. Why it matters: If you build or select evaluation suites, this means checking answer derivability and participant-separated splits can change whether a model score is interpretable before any model comparison begins. Evidence: E002, E004, E050. High confidence.

GraphInstruct is a new progressive benchmark for graph generation, with 900 instructions arranged across six constraint levels and 1,782 algorithmically synthesized reference solutions in version 1.1. It scores outputs on five dimensions using deterministic metrics and releases the dataset, raw model responses, per-instance scores, reference pools, and a code snapshot. Why it matters: If you are comparing models that must produce structured graphs, this provides more diagnostic information than a single pass rate: performance can be separated by constraint difficulty and scoring dimension, while the released responses and code support result inspection and reruns. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

SEBGen is a new framework that generates software-engineering agent tasks from code repositories and updates its generation strategies through an evolution loop. It scores candidate strategies across quality, novelty, difficulty coverage, skill diversity, and evolution potential rather than keeping one fixed task collection. Why it matters: If you maintain an agent benchmark, this changes the choice between a stable test set and a renewable one. SEBGen offers a concrete design for producing new tasks as existing sets become less discriminating, although the captured description does not establish how well its generated tasks hold up under independent validation. Evidence: E009. Medium confidence.

The new unsafe-eval leaderboard dataset publishes the underlying results for prompt-safety evaluations, pins every benchmark to a fixed dataset revision, and records one result file per run with scores, token use, and cost. Why it matters: If you are choosing safety classifiers or general-purpose models, this lets you examine operating cost alongside scores and rerun the same prompt revision, reducing ambiguity caused by silent dataset changes or leaderboard-only reporting. Evidence: E020. High confidence.
bullets_zh: Unreachable Oracles 引入了一种离线审计方法，用于检查每个基准答案是否确实能从智能体接收到的信息中推导出来。其规则通过一组明确声明的有限许可推导，同时追踪目标值和每个构造步骤。QAMQOR 和 radarvitals-audit 揭示了由参与者重叠引发的相关测试泄漏问题：分数可能反映的是对某个儿童、会话或受试者的识别，而非预期能力。这些发布共同表明，基准有效性已成为本次收录信息流中反复出现的设计压力。Why it matters: 如果你在构建或选择评测套件，这意味着，在开始任何模型比较之前，检查答案的可推导性以及按参与者隔离的数据划分，可能会改变模型分数是否具有可解释性。Evidence: E002, E004, E050. High confidence.

GraphInstruct 是一个新的渐进式图生成基准，包含按六个约束级别编排的 900 条指令，以及版本 1.1 中通过算法合成的 1,782 个参考解。它使用确定性指标从五个维度对输出进行评分，并发布数据集、原始模型响应、逐实例分数、参考池和代码快照。Why it matters: 如果你在比较必须生成结构化图的模型，它能提供比单一通过率更多的诊断信息：可按约束难度和评分维度拆分性能，而已发布的响应和代码则支持检查结果和重新运行。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

SEBGen 是一个新框架，可从代码仓库生成软件工程智能体任务，并通过演化循环更新其生成策略。它从质量、新颖性、难度覆盖、技能多样性和演化潜力等方面对候选策略进行评分，而不是维持一个固定的任务集合。Why it matters: 如果你在维护智能体基准，这会改变在稳定测试集与可持续更新测试集之间的选择。随着现有任务集的区分能力下降，SEBGen 提供了一种生成新任务的具体设计，但本次收录的描述并未证明其生成的任务在独立验证下表现如何。Evidence: E009. Medium confidence.

新的 unsafe-eval 排行榜数据集发布了提示安全评测的底层结果，将每个基准固定到特定的数据集修订版本，并为每次运行记录一个结果文件，其中包含分数、令牌用量和成本。Why it matters: 如果你在选择安全分类器或通用模型，这让你可以在查看分数的同时考察运行成本，并基于相同的提示修订版本重新运行，从而减少由数据集静默变更或仅通过排行榜报告所造成的歧义。Evidence: E020. High confidence.
briefing.caveat: This briefing covers 143 ranked evidence records selected from 624 captured artifacts, so it does not represent a review of the full daily corpus or the wider AI field. OpenReview and Brave were unavailable, and several attention collectors had unread or stale records. The feed also lacks enough comparable history to assess category-share movement.

evidence_items.summary: Credit card fraud detection is a critical problem in financial security, yet real-world deployment scenarios often lack labeled fraud samples at initial stages, making unsupervised anomaly detection an appealing approach. However, the comparative performance of different unsupervised detectors under varying training data compositions—whether trained exclusively on normal transactions or on mixed data containing unlabeled frauds—remains insufficiently studied. This paper presents a head-to-head benchmark of five unsupervised anomaly detectors—Mahalanobis distance, Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor (LOF), One-Class SVM, and Elliptic Envelope—on the publicly available ULB Credit Card Fraud Detection dataset. Each detector is evaluated under two training protocols: novelty detection (trained solely on normal transactions) and outlier detection (trained on the full dataset containing both normal and fraudulent samples). Performance is measured using PR-AUC, Precision@k, and recall at low false positive rates. Results show that Mahalanobis distance and LOF achieve strong performance under the novelty detection protocol (PR-AUC > 0.73) but suffer catastrophic degradation when trained on mixed data, with PR-AUC dropping by 0.57 and 0.72 respectively. Isolation Forest gives solid and reliable results on both two tested protocols, and its PR-AUC score increases slightly from 0.3953 to 0.4432. After parameter adjustment (with parameters set as support fraction=0.9, contamination=0.01), Elliptic Envelope gets moderate performance (PR-AUC≈0.37) and is almost insensible to protocol changes. The conclusions obtained in this part can provide actual instruction for choosing unsupervised detectors to be used in real fraud detection systems working under various conditions of label availability and data quality.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Anomaly Detectors for Credit Card Fraud under Two Training Protocols

evidence_items.summary: A tool-migration benchmark for LLM agents contains two objects that are easy to conflate: the behaviour under test and the oracle that scores it. This work asks whether the latter is well formed. We operationalize oracle identifiability under declared information rights at the level of the individual item: a ground-truth item is reachable only if its target value and every construction step are derivable, under a declared finite derivation grammar, from the information granted before the method's first call. We implement this criterion as a deterministic offline auditor with typed outcomes. Applied to a self-authored synthetic tool-drift benchmark, the audit finds 50 of 310 argument-pair items unreachable (16.1%), concentrated in two drift families. A separate 45-item required-field audit finds 20 additional unreachable items, reducing strict complete-call retention to zero in two families. Four derivation-grammar configurations reproduce the same 260/10/40 reachable/target-absent/convention-unobservable split. Twenty hand-adjudicated real Model Context Protocol version pairs are representable in the audit schema and none is flagged; however, 15 of the 20 depend on hand-supplied observability annotations and therefore do not constitute an independent specificity estimate. After invalid items are excluded, the retained evaluation surface is also too small to satisfy the preregistered precision and power criterion for the intended comparative study. The results argue that oracle validity should be checked before agent performance is interpreted: a benchmark should declare its information rights, audit every ground-truth target for derivability, and verify that the retained evaluation surface remains adequate for the intended comparison.
evidence_items.title: Unreachable Oracles: Auditing Ground-Truth Derivability in a Synthetic Tool-Drift Benchmark for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: GraphInstruct is a progressive benchmark for instruction-following graph generation by large language models. Version 1.0, on which the main experiments run, organizes 800 instructions into six constraint-type levels (L0 to L5) with 1,582 algorithmically synthesized reference solutions; version 1.1 adds 100 L5 items, for 900 instructions and 1,782 reference solutions. Outputs are scored on five dimensions with deterministic metrics, and two reference pools are included. This record holds the dataset, the raw model responses, the per-instance scores, and a snapshot of the code repository at the release commit. All archives extract into one folder and use the relative paths of the repository: GraphInstruct-1.1.0-dataset.tar.gz: the dataset alone (instructions, reference solutions, reference pools, the additional L5 items, the stress subset, the paraphrased instructions, the unchanged files of version 1.0, Croissant metadata, datasheet, data format description, data licence).- GraphInstruct-1.1.0-repository.tar.gz: every file of the repository at the release commit (dataset, evaluator, scripts, tests, per-instance quality scores, expected table fragments of the paper).- GraphInstruct-1.1.0-raw-responses-main.tar.gz: raw model responses of the 45 runs of the baseline survey as reviewed. Its four GPT-3.5 runs were served by a third-party relay and are superseded by the official GPT-3.5 runs in the next archive.- GraphInstruct-1.1.0-raw-responses-extended.tar.gz: all other raw model responses (the official GPT-3.5 runs, extended model panel, method runs and ablations, additional L5 items, paraphrased instructions, regenerated runs).- SHA256SUMS.txt and MANIFEST.tsv: checksums of the archives and of every archived file.

evidence_items.summary: Reliable engagement recognition is important for adaptive robot-assisted autism therapy (RAAT). However, progress remains constrained by the scarcity of publicly available benchmarks evaluated under realistic deployment conditions. Existing studies commonly adopt random train–test splits, which can inflate reported performance because recordings from the same child or therapy session may appear in both the training and test sets. To address this gap, we introduce QAMQOR, a benchmark dataset for engagement recognition collected during RAAT sessions with 34 children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), aged 3 − 12 years. The dataset includes visual engagement annotations derived from therapy session videos and feature representations extracted using two pose-estimation frameworks. The QAMQOR dataset defines four clinically relevant evaluation protocols based on Random, Child-Independent, Session-Independent, and Activity-Independent splits. These evaluation protocols assess model generalization to unseen children, therapy sessions and activity tasks. We benchmark classical machine learning classifiers together with temporal and sequence-learning baselines for both binary and multi-class engagement recognition. Experimental results show that the evaluation protocol influenced reported performance to a degree comparable to, and for fine-grained engagement classification exceeding, the influence of classifier selection: mean macro-F1 varied by 0.12 across the four protocols in the multi-class task, against 0.07 across discriminative classifiers. The Child-Independent split proved substantially more challenging than the Random split. Under the same conditions (windows, protocols, training schedule and untuned hyperparameters) a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) did not outperform the classical baselines.
evidence_items.title: QAMQOR: a benchmark dataset for engagement recognition in robot-assisted autism therapy

evidence_items.summary: The African mining industry continues to face a serious communication gap between technical safety documentation and the language used by the workforce. Safety manuals, operating procedures, and regulatory guidance are often produced in English or French, while many workers communicate in isiZulu, chiShona, and other local languages. This mismatch is not just inconvenient; it can be dangerous in safety-critical settings where misunderstandings may contribute to preventable incidents. This paper reports on Talk MINING, a domain-adapted multilingual large language model built on InkubaLM and trained on mining-specific text, question–answer pairs, and multimodal hazard data. The model was developed using Hugging Face tools and evaluated with both quantitative and qualitative methods. Results show a marked improvement over the baseline model, with overall accuracy rising from below 50% to 82%, and strong gains across isiZulu, chiShona, and English. The project also includes a web-based prototype that allows users to take photos of mining conditions and receive guidance in a local language. This paper presents the full pipeline for Talk MINING, including document preparation, translation and localization, model training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and validation. Beyond benchmark performance, the system is designed for practical deployment in environments where connectivity is limited and literacy levels vary—supporting both text queries and image-based hazard input through a mobile-ready prototype. The work contributes a reproducible pipeline, a curated multilingual mining corpus, and an open evaluation framework that can serve as a foundation for extending domain-adapted AI to other African languages and safety-critical industries. Ultimately, Talk MINING demonstrates that closing the language gap in mining safety is not only technically feasible but achievable with relatively modest model size when domain adaptation is done rigorously.
evidence_items.title: A Domain-Adapted Multilingual Large Language Model for Mining Safety in African Languages

evidence_items.summary: Phishing URL detection using machine learning has achieved near-perfect accuracy on popular benchmark datasets, but the extent to which these results generalize across datasets remains unclear. We train a Random Forest classifier on the PhiUSIIL phishing URL dataset (235,795 records) and evaluate it on the UCI Phishing Websites dataset (11,055 records), after mapping a subset of PhiUSIIL features into the UCI feature space. In-domain, our model achieves balanced accuracy of 0.9999 on a domain-separated PhiUSIIL test split and 0.9979 for a URL-lexical-feature-only variant. On the external UCI dataset, balanced accuracy drops to 0.9530 (full numeric) and 0.6753 (transfer experiment using 10 mapped features), with a generalization gap of 0.287. We further analyze 64 feature-vector groups with conflicting labels in the UCI dataset and show that a trained model is near chance-level on those rows, indicating an irreducible label-noise ceiling rather than a model deficiency. Our results argue that high in-domain performance is insufficient evidence of real-world reliability and that multi-dataset evaluation should be standard practice for phishing detectors.
evidence_items.title: Explainable and Robust Machine Learning for Phishing URL Detection: A Cross-Dataset Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Static software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench suffer from three fundamental limitations: task sets are fixed and become saturated as model capabilities rapidly improve; expert construction is costly and slow; and difficulty levels cannot adapt to evolving model abilities. We present SEBGen, a self-evolving benchmark generation framework that synthesizes evaluation tasks from code repositories and continuously updates its generation strategies through an evolution loop. SEBGen introduces three key innovations: an explicit five-dimension exploration value evaluator that quantitatively scores generation strategies across quality, novelty, difficulty coverage, skill diversity, and evolution potential, replacing implicit LLM judgments; a hybrid validation pipeline combining three mechanical checks (schema, compile, functional), an LLM-based semantic assessment, and a repeated-judgment gate; and a self-evolving loop with archive-based experience accumulation, sigmoid-scaled parent selection, and LLM-driven strategy mutation. On a synthetic corpus, SEBGen achieves a 96 percent stage-level validation pass rate (E1; 48/50 stage observations) and preserves generation quality through the evolution loop while showing no measurable improvement over a budget-matched non-evolution baseline. On a real repository, it generates candidate benchmark tasks from all six tqdm commits that passed the schema and LLM-based screening stages, although the compile and functional stages could not be executed because these tasks carry no test patch. A judge-level comparison against SWE-bench Lite, partially corroborated by an independent judge from a different model family (Qwen), places generated real repository tasks below expert-constructed tasks (0.48 vs. 0.83 under deepseek-chat; 0.55 vs. 0.78 under qwen-plus, mean of two passes).
evidence_items.title: SEBGen: A Self-Evolving Benchmark Generation Framework for Software Engineering Agents

evidence_items.summary: We combine GeneNetwork's 1TB structured database with its metadata as an RDF graph and an associated literature corpus. We benchmark frontier and local LLMs querying it through four architectures: document, graph and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of the three. We evaluate them on 40 domain specific expert-curated questions with a new metric: the satisfaction frequency psi (psi, i.e, the share of questions answered with precision and recall of at least 70% or an f1 of at least 60%). psi ranks systems the same way precision, recall and f1 -- a machine learning metric built from the harmonic mean of precision and recall -- but is easier to read and assess for humans. System architecture had a large effect: with full use of Claude Opus 4.8 the plain document RAG of our earlier GNQA system had a psi of 36% against 86% for our new combined tools. Delegating most of the work from Claude Opus 4.8 to a local model halved query costs while still reaching a psi of 59%.

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used both as recommenders and to explain recommendations, yet producing faithful, user-centric explanations and evaluating them rigorously remain open problems, compounded by a documented reproducibility crisis in recommender systems research. In this work we formalise recommendation as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and propose a unified, three-tier agentic framework that couples a simulation environment (RecoWorld), a reproducible policy engine (RecBole), and a cognitive LLM user agent. As an offline, single-turn validation of this framework on the MovieLens-32M dataset, we benchmark preliminary single-epoch checkpoints of traditional policies (Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), Convolutional Neural Collaborative Filtering and Neural Matrix Factorisation (NeuMF)), generate LLM-based explanations from the BPR recommendations and score them with quantitative diversity, faithfulness, counterfactual and readability metrics over roughly one million user-item pairs, and run an LLM-as-user interview simulation in which explanations produced by a Qwen2.5 explainer are assessed by a Llama-3 respondent through a six-criterion explanation-quality survey; a controlled comparison on 2000 users shows that replacing BPR with the more accurate NeuMF policy leaves these survey scores practically unchanged. The generated explanations prove highly faithful (feature precision 0.9996, sufficiency 0.9999) and user-tailored explanations (unique-sentence ratio 0.9978), and simulated users rate clarity highest (3.86/5) yet trust lowest (2.60/5). Faithful template explanations are, therefore, trusted less than they are understood, motivating a shift towards controllable generative explanation and scalable simulated evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Simulating Users to Evaluate LLM-Generated Explanations in Recommender Systems: A Unified Agentic Framework and Empirical Study with Preliminary Results

evidence_items.summary: Compliance-Aware Credit-agent Evaluation (CACE-Bench): a synthetic, reproducible benchmark and generator for evaluating LLM-agent credit pipelines, and the self-evolution of such pipelines, under auditability constraints. No production credit data is used; the only real records are the 1,000 applications of the public, anonymised Statlog German Credit data (UCI, CC BY 4.0), shipped with a SHA-256 check. Version 0.7.0 runs the regulatory-shift track on those applicants (evolve real.py; evolve.py unchanged) with a 700/300 split of applicants per seed, so no evaluated applicant is in the gate's pool. Over 90 runs the gated dual loop admitted 171 of 6874 candidate changes with 0 harmful admissions; the same loops without the gate admitted 228 harmful changes and ended with a missed-flag rate above 10 percent in 29 of 90 runs. The dual loop reached the oracle harness in 80 of 80 runs outside the scope-high cell and in 0 of 10 within it, where the fixed tolerance blocks the correct change (9 of 10 at epsilon = 0.01); there the residual false positives fall unevenly, by +2.3 percentage points for women and +4.2 for applicants under 25 beyond the oracle's own gap. Version 0.7.0 also adds a language-model proposer (proposer llm.py) with a response cache keyed by SHA-256 for exact replay. In a pilot of 15 runs (mid severity, 5 seeds; Claude Haiku 4.5 as proposer, model version and temperature not pinned, reproducible from the released cache) both loops ended at the correct harness, but without the gate 13 admissions were harmful and missed flags during adaptation reached 22.3 percent in the scope family, against 0 and 2.0 percent with the gate.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Predicting properties from coordinate–category data—sets of vectors paired with categorical information—is fundamental to computational science, manifesting in materials science as predicting formation energies or elastic moduli from crystal structures. While large language models (LLMs) have increasingly been applied to such tasks, optimal strategies for achieving reliable predictions remain elusive. Here we report fundamental limitations in LLM’s ability to learn from coordinate information in coordinate–category data. Through systematic experiments using synthetic datasets with tunable coordinate and category contributions, and a comprehensive benchmarking framework (MatText), we find that LLMs consistently fail to capture coordinate information while excelling at category patterns. This geometric blindness persists regardless of model size (up to 70 billion parameters), dataset scale (up to 2 × 10 6 structures) or text representation strategy. For material property prediction tasks dominated by structural effects, specialized geometric architectures consistently outperform LLMs, as evidenced by a clear ‘Graph Neural Network Language Model (GNN-LM) wall’ in performance benchmarks. Our analysis provides concrete guidelines for architecture selection in scientific machine learning.
evidence_items.title: Less can be more for predicting properties with large language models

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This study aims to develop and validate a high-quality voice dataset for dysphonia therapy using a standardized, video-guided recording protocol comprising a range of therapeutic voice exercises. The dataset is designed to support the development of digital health applications that enable home-based voice training with real-time biofeedback, thereby addressing current challenges in speech-language pathology, including limited access to therapy and the need for scalable, patient-centered interventions. Methods: A voice dataset was collected from adult participants performing voice therapy exercises in German, recorded via smartphone and in-ear microphones under standardized conditions. In addition to acoustic data collection, participants evaluated the recording procedure and video-guided exercise instructions. Acoustic analyses of pitch (Hz), intensity (dB), and Cepstral Peak Prominence (CPP) were conducted using Praat, with data grouped by age and sex. Correlation analyses were performed to assess the consistency of recordings across participants and exercises. Results: The resulting dataset comprises recordings from 175 adults, totaling approximately 6.6 GB of audio data, with a subset made available as open access. Participants reported high overall acceptance of the recording procedure and instructional videos, while also identifying areas for improvement, particularly regarding pacing and clarity. Acoustic and correlation analyses demonstrated exercise-specific variations in CPP, pitch and intensity, as well as systematic differences across age and gender groups, indicating both variability and structured consistency within the dataset. Conclusion: The dataset represents a novel resource for digital voice therapy, particularly due to its focus on structured therapeutic exercises in German.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objective To characterise the reporting completeness of clinical trials involving large language model (LLM) interventions using established reporting guidelines. Design Systematic review and meta-research analysis. Data sources Bibliographic databases (Embase, Medline, and CENTRAL) were searched for trial reports and protocols, and trial registries (ClinicalTrials.gov and World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were searched for trial registrations published from 1 January 2017 to 6 December 2025. Eligibility criteria Trial reports, trial protocols, and trial registrations describing clinical trials of LLM interventions in medicine. LLM interventions used for a healthcare function in a clinical trial setting included patient education, clinical documentation, communication support, triage, care navigation, management recommendations, or clinical decision support. Eligible studies prospectively assigned human participants to the intervention and evaluated a health related biomedical or behavioural outcome. Main outcome measures Overall study level and item level reporting completeness assessed using reporting guidelines matched to study design and purpose, including TRIPOD-LLM (Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis—LLM), CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) 2025 and CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT (Standard Protocol Items: Recommendations for Interventional Trials) 2025 and SPIRIT-AI, CHART (Chatbot Assessment Reporting Tool), and the WHO Trial Registration Dataset (version 1.3.1). Two reviewers independently screened and extracted trial and intervention characteristics, and three calibrated raters assessed item level reporting completeness. Results The systematic search yielded 461 records, including 68 trial reports, 15 protocols, and 378 registrations.
evidence_items.title: Reporting completeness of clinical trials evaluating large language model interventions in medicine: systematic review

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate medical assessment items, but their reliability for disease-specific question writing remains uncertain. We benchmarked seven LLMs for epilepsy single-best-answer multiple-choice question generation under a standardized blueprint, focusing on structural compliance, clinical accuracy, expert-rated quality and educational usability. Methods Each model completed the same 60 prespecified tasks spanning foundational knowledge, clinical cases, treatment decision-making, and diagnostic evaluation and longitudinal management, yielding 420 questions. Tasks were delivered through an identical single-turn prompt without model-specific optimization, web search or external tools. Objective evaluation assessed structural compliance, keyed-answer accuracy, textual characteristics and response time. Two blinded clinical reviewers independently rated content rigor, clarity, distractor quality, educational usefulness, cognitive alignment and overall usability on five-point scales. Results After one standardized corrective prompt, all 420 questions met structural requirements, although first-pass compliance ranged from 83.33% to 100%. Keyed-answer accuracy varied substantially, from 61.67% to 98.33%, with Claude-5 achieving the highest accuracy. GPT-5.6 obtained the highest composite expert score (median, 3.75), followed by Claude-5 (3.67) and Kimi-K3 (3.50). Distractor quality was a common limitation, with median scores of only 2–3 across models. Only 2 of 420 questions (0.48%) were judged directly usable without revision, both generated by GPT-5.6; 119 (28.33%) were usable after minor revision and 299 (71.19%) required substantial revision. Longer outputs were associated with better cognitive alignment but not with content rigor or clarity, while response time was unrelated to overall usability.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging large language models to generate multiple-choice questions for epilepsy education

evidence_items.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) plays a central role in global food and nutritional security, but its productivity is challenged by biotic and abiotic stresses. Its large, polyploid genome and extensive repetitive sequences complicate the identification of genetic variation and the dissection of complex agronomic traits. This review examines emerging genomic resources and the complementary contributions of transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and epigenomics to wheat improvement. High-throughput genotyping platforms, including SNP arrays, genotyping-by-sequencing and DArTseq, facilitate genetic diversity analysis and the identification of genomic regions associated with agronomic traits. Pan-genome approaches extend analyses beyond a single reference assembly by capturing structural, copy-number and presence–absence variation. Functional omics studies provide information on transcriptional regulation, protein responses, metabolite accumulation and chromatin-associated mechanisms involved in development and stress adaptation. The review also considers the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning for integrating complex datasets, predicting yield-related traits, automating phenotypic assessment and supporting genomic selection. Examples from wheat demonstrate the potential value of combining molecular information with computational approaches, although the reliability of predictions depends on data quality, representation and appropriate validation. Together, these advances provide complementary tools for identifying candidate genes and interpreting genotype–phenotype relationships. Their integration with reliable phenotypic information and established breeding practices may support more efficient wheat improvement while acknowledging the technical and biological challenges of translating molecular findings into breeding outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Advancing Wheat Improvement through Multi-Omics and Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Predicting time-to-conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a critical clinical challenge. Most survival analyses rely on static baseline variables, ignoring the temporal dynamics of serial neuroimaging. We benchmark seven survival model families using a novel temporal MRI descriptor pipeline on ADNI. Methods: A cohort of 661 MCI patients (250 conversion events, 37.8%, median follow-up 42.0 months) was constructed from ADNI. FreeSurfer volumetrics of six brain regions were summarised into three time-based descriptors each (atrophy rate, trajectory variability σ, and time-weighted cumulative mean μ) under strict anti-leakage constraints, yielding 18 neuroimaging features which, combined with six clinical variables (age, sex, education, MMSE, ADAS-13, and APOE-ε4), form a 24-dimensional covariate vector. Cox PH, Weibull AFT, Exponential, RSF, GBST, DeepSurv, and DeepHit were evaluated under stratified 5-fold cross-validation and assessed on an independent OASIS-3 cohort (n=78) as an exploratory analysis. Results: All seven models achieved C-index 0.853–0.863 (Δ=0.010), with Cox PH reaching 0.863±0.027 using only routine structural MRI. Time-dependent AUC ranged from 0.856 (12 months) to 0.938 (48 months). Risk stratification by quartile yielded highly separated Kaplan-Meier curves (log-rank p<0.001). On OASIS-3 (n=78, exploratory), classical models showed preliminary cross-cohort consistency (Weibull AFT 0.760±0.063, RSF 0.759±0.049), while deep learning degraded substantially (DeepSurv 0.551±0.116); these results are hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as confirmatory given the small per-fold sample size (EPV ≈ 1). Conclusions: The temporal MRI descriptor pipeline achieves a C-index of 0.863 using only routine structural MRI, without PET or CSF biomarkers, demonstrating strong discriminative performance on ADNI MCI-to-AD conversion.
evidence_items.title: Predicting MCI-to-Alzheimer’s Conversion: A Systematic Benchmark of Classical, Machine Learning, and Deep Survival Models

evidence_items.summary: In this study, a high-fidelity multi-physics framework was established through the direct link between the continuous energy Monte Carlo (MC) neutronics code McCARD and the subchannel thermal-hydraulic (T/H) analysis code MATRA. A relaxation scheme suppressed numerical oscillations due to the stochastic nature of the MC method and ensured stable convergence of the Picard iteration. The SMART benchmark problems served to evaluate the accuracy and numerical stability of the developed system through a stepwise verification procedure. First, closed-channel calculations assessed the physical consistency of the fundamental T/H models in the two codes. The subsequent open-channel calculations quantified the effects of cross-flow and turbulent inter-channel exchange. The numerical results show that explicit consideration of lateral heat and mass transfer between adjacent subchannels substantially reduces local coolant-temperature peaks and produces temperature distributions that more closely represent the relevant physical phenomena. The coupled framework also captures distinct pin-wise power variations, particularly near the periphery, due to subchannel-scale T/H feedback that the single-physics model does not account for. Consequently, this study demonstrates that the McCARD/MATRA external multi-physics code system can represent the multi-physics phenomena required for high-fidelity safety analyses and provides a reliable technical basis for SMR design optimization.
evidence_items.title: Multi-Physics Analysis of SMART Small Modular Reactor Benchmark Problems Using the Coupled McCARD/MATRA Code System

evidence_items.summary: Human-robot collaboration has relied on task models that are specified in advance for each product. Embodied foundation models and agentic artificial intelligence change this premise, because a robot can now interpret an open goal, plan, act, monitor the outcome and recover from failure. This review examines what that change means for collaboration. A critical narrative review was conducted over 231 sources. Embodied intelligence, agentic intelligence, autonomy and collaboration are distinguished, and four collaboration modes are defined by the roles of the human and the robot. Four system architectures are compared: modular agentic, end-to-end embodied, hierarchical agentic embodied, and human-centred shared autonomy. Six groups of enabling technologies and five collaboration mechanisms, from autonomy allocation to failure recovery, are analysed. Applications in six domains, from manufacturing to domestic service, are assessed by the maturity of their evidence. Reported systems are validated mainly on single cells and short tasks, human factors are measured in few studies, and verified safety layers remain separate from learned reasoning. An evaluation framework and research directions for seven open challenges are proposed. The review gives researchers and system builders a basis for bringing embodied and agentic AI into human-robot collaboration and for evaluating the systems that result.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Embodied AI for Human–Robot Collaboration: Architectures, Technologies, and Future Directions

evidence_items.summary:
This study critically evaluates existing legislations to examine its scope and limitations regarding the sustainability of market design (MD) and effective regulation of abuse of dominant position (ADP) to protect consumer sovereignty in India. It aims to identify principal factors causing gradual shrinkage of the Indian telecommunications and aviation sectors and to examine the role of concerned market regulators from legal and policy design perspectives to identify mechanisms adopted to keep competitiveness viable which is a quid pro quo for economic development and consumer-welfare. The methodology is doctrinal, qualitative and analytical.
 
 
 
 This study adopts a doctrinal legal research design employing qualitative analysis through the interpretation of provisions, regulatory instruments, judicial decisions, official market studies, policy documents and authoritative secondary literature and therefore does not seek to establish statistically validated causal relationships between regulatory intervention and market concentration. The qualitative nature of the study lies in the interpretative examination of legal and institutional frameworks rather than empirical qualitative methods such as interviews, surveys or thematic coding. Therefore, the original contribution is analytical and inferential. Findings consequently identify patterns, regulatory gaps and legally relevant relationships that may contribute to understanding competitive outcomes, without claiming that regulatory failure is the definitive cause of market concentration. It is to be clarified that telecom- and aviation-related data are used as sectoral illustrations and documentary bases for concentration analysis rather than as statistically representative empirical case studies. The Competition Commission of India’s (CCI's) 2009 aviation sector market study is referred to here only as a historical benchmark rather than as evidence of current market structure. Since the core objective of this study is to evaluate whether legislative objectives underlying the Competition Act, 2002 (CA) have been effectively realised over time, it is methodologically necessary to establish competitive conditions prevailing during the initial years of India's competition regime. The subsequent analysis therefore compares this historical benchmark with recent market statistics, regulatory reports and contemporary literature to examine the evolution of market concentration and institutional effectiveness. Justification for Cross-Sectoral Examination of Competition Issues: Telecom sector depends on extensive network and infrastructure, while the aviation sector is characterised by intense capital requirements and heavy infrastructure. However, there are many common characteristics from the competition issues, particularly, in terms of structural and economic characteristics. For examples; high capital intensity, limited number of market participants, large consumer bases, network-based industries, economies of scale, infrastructure-dependent operations, strategic importance to national development, strong potential for market consolidation and substantial consumer welfare impact, etc. are common in both sectors and therefore this study focuses on these sectors. Another reason for the selection of these sectors is the recent ostensible duopoly/monopoly of enterprises, exorbitant price or tariff hikes and cartelisation-like situations in both services areas. Therefore; this discussion is underpinned by the current market share of corporations and the factual details behind their emergence. Accordingly, the central focus of this study is not judicial cases but rather the correlated happenings and the role of the authorities in shaping the current telecom and aviation market design in India.
 
 
 
 The study finds that Indian laws provide a strong framework that is highly efficient in prohibiting ADP and capable of maintaining competitive viability while keeping MD intact. However, it seems that authorities have somewhat failed to operationalise legal policy and frameworks effectively have been unable to forecast adverse effects i a timely manner, and have not developed collaborative mechanisms to prevent current market concentration.
 
 
 
 The study’s core discussion is mainly focused on the said sectors and its legal perspective is limited to the Indian jurisdiction. Its results may be used as a case study for similar sectoral studies.
 
 
 
 The study contributes to the legal interpretation of the concept of ADP from competition sustainability and viability perspectives. This implication helps in interpreting the CA in light of dynamic and sustainability-based competition goals. The study highlights key common characteristics of the said sectors. It also contributes to policy reforms and institutional coordination.
 
 
 
 The research strongly highlights consumer welfare aspects, namely, fair pricing, service quality and convenient service accessibility, etc. It focuses on how dominance in network- and infrastructure-based industries may lead to monopoly/duopoly, the antithesis of competitive viability. The Indian Constitution envisages economic policies to discourage concentration of wealth. Therefore, this study highlights how enterprise dominance poses a potential risk of economic inequality.
 
 
 
 The study is original in the sense that prior research acknowledges concerns relating to market concentration, but there has been limited scholarly engagement with recent consolidation trends since 2020. Its originality lies in its challenge to the prevailing assumption that concentration of a sectoral market necessarily reflects inadequacies in legal policy/frameworks. However, it demonstrates through an analysis of publicly available market statistics, regulatory reports and legal materials, that the existing competition law (CL) framework is well designed to address anti-competitive practices (ACPs) Nevertheless, scholarly studies/professional-experts indicate a noticeable deterioration in competitive viability (CV) in the said sectors during this period which is not a normal market responses based on supply/demand theory. Therefore, this study argues that the major hindrance is not legislative insufficiency but shortcomings in regulatory enforcement, coordination and timely implementation of existing law. This enforcement gap has contributed to the weakening of competition sustainability posing challenges to the preservation of efficient/sustainable MD.
evidence_items.title: Competition law and sustainable market design: regulating dominant positions to preserve competitive viability in India's telecom and aviation sectors

evidence_items.summary: In this paper, we study physically grounded articulated 3D asset generation---moving the goal from reproducing how objects look to capturing how they move and function. Inspired by the literature on procedural and agentic generation, we present Artisan, a system that extends the latest method Articraft by introducing a multi-agent pipeline with physical simulation feedback, enabling comprehensive attributes beyond geometry, appearance, and physically plausible articulation, such as collision-free motion, stability under gravity, and accurate mass and material properties. Furthermore, we construct a unified benchmark spanning four key aspects: spatial fidelity, physical plausibility, downstream task performance, and overall quality. The benchmark encompasses 100 reference assets from ArtVIP and LightWheel, 50 stability prompts, and 50 ABO objects with reference masses, with protocols evaluating various metrics. Through extensive evaluation of more than 10 representative models, Artisan achieves competitive spatial fidelity while attaining the lowest collision rates and highest stability rates among the evaluated methods. Together, our system and benchmark establish insights for advancing 3D generation towards physically plausible, functionally usable assets.
evidence_items.title: Towards Physically Grounded Articulated 3D Assets: A Multi-Agent Pipeline and Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. The benchmark includes five agent profiles, twelve buyer personas, fifteen smartphone products across six price tiers, and four controlled experiments with 3 iterations totaling 13,680 sessions. Both sales-agent and buyer persona generations are grounded through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We introduce nine evaluation metrics grouped into three tiers: primary outcome metrics (CR, BRS, RIR), secondary quality metrics (SMS, PFS, ETI), and exploratory metrics planned for future reporting (ITS, ARI, SPI). Our evaluation combines automated LLM-as-judge scoring with internal human assessment (n = 50, \k{appa} = 0.71, Pearson r = 0.81 with BRS).
evidence_items.title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.
evidence_items.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks

This English-language research monograph develops a falsifiable program for conceptual emergence and generative intelligence. Its research three-coupling is Interaction Generation × New-Function Identification × Counterfactual Verification. The proposed emergence expression compares held-out capability improvement with the strongest viable baseline and a contamination penalty, with all terms requiring operational definition and appropriate normalization before use. RESEARCH DESIGN The volume studies both smooth scaling and possible discontinuities, evaluation-metric sensitivity, training-data leakage, compositional generalization, simple-rule baselines, factorial component ablation, multi-agent collaboration, correlated errors, human-AI complementarity, multimodal grounding, causal interventions, tool-dependence, calibration, cross-model reproducibility, governance, and intergenerational handoff. A claimed capability must survive preregistered unseen tasks, strong comparators, counterfactual perturbations and independent reproduction. A fluent explanation, a generated new term or a model's assertion of consciousness is not evidence of functional emergence. evidence_items.summary: Where did the first interpreter come from? Conventional wisdom is that living things interpret the world, to survive. I argue the opposite. The world interprets the actions of the living, to determine who survives. I assume only a set of distinctions, because without distinction there is nought. A timeline is a sequence of distinctions. Each timeline ranks things by persistence, a ranking I call the Cosmic Ought. Every timeline is an opinion about what ought to persist. Living things are attracted to whatever lets them persist. I call this valence. I argue the objects and properties a living thing recognises are patterns of valence, so evaluation precedes neutral representation. I prove each mental thing a living thing learns lowers its persistence rank, unless it aligns with the Cosmic Ought. Objects and properties are thus chords in a symphony of valence, played by an orchestra of cells, conducted by time.
evidence_items.title: Every Timeline Is an Opinion

evidence_items.summary: This deposit contains the complete analysis code and the de-identified, specimen-level dataset underlying every statistic reported in the study "Beyond organoids: restoring the value of patient-derived two-dimensional colorectal cancer models" (Linnebacher et al.). The study is a single-centre observational analysis of the establishment of two-dimensional (2D) adherent cell lines from 158 colorectal cancer specimens (primary tumour tissue and patient-derived xenografts) held in the HROC biobank, University Medical Center Rostock. It evaluates twelve culture conditions across four media formulations with and without the ROCK inhibitor Y-27632, and tests whether establishment success can be predicted from clinical, histopathological or molecular parameters. The repository includes two Python scripts and one dataset: - analysis.py — primary analysis (cohort description, per-condition rates, primary-vs-PDX comparison, paired Y-27632 analysis, modern-vs-historical media, contamination, matched-pair concordance, the 13-variable predictor battery across three cohorts, multivariate modelling, and a contamination-handling sensitivity analysis). It begins with a data-integrity check that halts if the clinical and culture data disagree. - predictor enhanced.py — extended analyses: effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals, adjustment for the number of PDX culture attempts, Firth penalized logistic regression for low-prevalence molecular markers, post-hoc detectability, and media-specificity tests. - HROC predictor dataset cleaned.xlsx — de-identified specimen-level dataset (157 clinically annotated specimens) with culture outcomes, clinical/histopathological/molecular annotation and survival intervals. It contains no direct identifiers. Running the scripts reproduces all values in the main text, Tables 1–4, Figures 1–2, and the supplementary analyses. Requires Python 3.12 with pandas, numpy, scipy, statsmodels and openpyxl.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Battery swapping enables rapid energy replenishment for light electric vehicles (LEVs), but high-turnover pack circulation requires reliable pack-level health and remaining useful life ( RUL ) assessment. Publicly reusable longitudinal ageing datasets for complete LEV packs remain scarce. We develop a proxy-pack data-generation and learning framework that organizes independently tested cell-ageing records into fixed-member trajectories representing a 48 V-class 16-series configuration. Each trajectory retains 16 physical-cell identities over their common-cycle sequence. Cycle-level member states are aggregated into pack features for predicting a conservative minimum-member proxy RUL, with test barcodes isolated before combinatorial augmentation. Across ten barcode-level splits in each of three source cohorts, same-source tests with endpoints within the augmented training lifetime range achieved a median R² of 0.909 and a median Spearman correlation of 0.997. Tests beyond this range retained strong degradation ordering but showed larger absolute errors. A secondary mixed-source audit of 80 held-out trajectories achieved a median R² of 0.714 and a median Spearman correlation of 0.992. A matched composition-control analysis yielded a median R² by change of -0.015 after balancing barcode reuse and limiting composition overlap, indicating limited sensitivity to training-composition sampling. A complementary physical audit using one fixed 12S3P pack confirmed cell-to-branch-to-pack electrical closure and revealed persistent voltage limitation and migration of the maximum-temperature location. Proxy-pack generation therefore provides a reproducible approach for constructing longitudinal member-aware benchmarks from cell-ageing records and evaluating pack-health and RUL models across varied compositions and lifetime conditions.
evidence_items.title: Longitudinal proxy pack benchmark generation for remaining useful life assessment of light electric vehicle battery packs in swapping systems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The rapid deployment of AI-native applications in complex wellbore operations requires unified, high-quality data integration to sustain continuous model evolution and reliable asset lifecycle management. However, heterogeneity in standards, semantics, and system architectures across legacy operational datasets limits their immediate applicability for dynamic and agile AI workflows. In alignment with the digital transformation priorities on information management, knowledge integration, and emerging technology implementations, this study develops a Human- and Entity-Centric Agentic Travelling Approach (HATA) for constructing dynamic-static ontology that support adaptive, cross-scenario data integration. This supports the energy transformation by enabling adaptive data integration for complex decision scenarios, validated through 3 typical types of downhole failure cases. HATA introduces a self-organising ontology construction framework composed of three specialised AI agents configured to address data quality challenges in knowledge modelling, and semantic enabled data integration. The planner interprets engineer-determined themes and decomposes them into ontology construction tasks; the traveller explores latent representational spaces to generate ontology candidates optimised for scenario relevance; and the supervisor assesses structural and semantic consistency, providing iterative feedback to guide refinement. The approach was evaluated using operational datasets (2021-2024) from 45 shale-oil wellbores in western China, focusing on wax deposition, scaling, and pump leakage, with corresponding financial management.
evidence_items.title: An Ontology Construction Framework for Asset Lifecycle Management: Agentic Travelling Approach with Field Application in Shale Oil Wellbore Maintenance

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: Data for Performance evaluation of the Alphasense OPC-N3 and Plantower PMS5003 sensor in measuring dust events in the Salt Lake Valley, Utah This data file was used to estimate the performance of the Alphasense OPC-N3 and PMS5003 sensor in measuring ambient PM10, especially during dust events, and to obtain correction factors to correct the PMS5003 data. During April 2022, the OPC-N3 and PMS5003 sensors were collocated with federal equivalent method (FEM)at two Utah Division of Air Quality (UDAQ) sites: Hawthorne (HW) station and Environmental Quality (EQ) station. One residential site (RS)was also tested, with OPC-N3 and PMS5003 collocated with GRIMM portable aerosol spectrophotometer. The FEM data (PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations) and meteorological parameters (wind speed, wind direction, relative humidity, and temperature) for the two UDAQ sites were downloaded from the EPA website. The Excel sheet contained all the raw data and the processed data. The FEM, OPC-N3, and PMS5003 measurements were labeled as FEM-YYY, OPC-YYY, and PMS-YYY, where YYY represents the sites nomenclature, i.e., HW, EQ, and RS. The sheet labeled "HW", "RS", and," EQ" contained the raw measurements (meteorological, PM10, and PM2.5 (whenever applicable)) for the sites. The sheet" PM-ratio-based correlation" provided the data used to get the PM-ratio-based correlation. Briefly, based on the ratio of FEM-HW PM2.5/PM10, the FEM-HW and PMS-HW PM10 measurements were segregated into six bins: PM2.5/PM10: 0.7. For each bin, the co-located PMS-HW PM10 concentrations were linearly regressed against the FEM-HW PM10 concentrations to obtain correction factors (slope and intercept). These correction factors were later used to correct the PMS PM10 concentrations at the other two locations (RS and EQ), presented in the sheets with labels "RS correction using GRIMM ratio", "RS correction using opc ratio" and "EQ corrected using EQ ratio".
evidence_items.title: Dataset for: Performance Evaluation of the Alphasense OPC-N3 and Plantower PMS5003 Sensor in Measuring Dust Events in the Salt Lake Valley, Utah

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the experimental dataset and R scripts generated during the development and optimization of an instant functional beverage powder formulated from cheese whey and Caqueteña pineapple (Ananas comosus L. Merr.) using spray-drying technology. The dataset includes the physicochemical characterization of raw materials (cheese whey and pineapple pulp), formulation design, spray-drying operating conditions, physicochemical and technological properties of the resulting powders, and sensory acceptance data of the reconstituted beverages evaluated by untrained panelists. Measured variables include pH, titratable acidity, density, fat, protein, moisture content, ash, water activity, °Brix, color coordinates (L , a , b ), powder yield, solubility, wettability, and hedonic sensory scores for appearance, color, aroma, body, acidity, and flavor. In addition, this repository provides the R scripts used for statistical analysis, including descriptive statistics, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), principal component analysis (PCA), heatmap visualization, and multivariate exploratory modeling. The integration of experimental data and reproducible analytical code provides a reliable computational framework for the study of spray-dried dairy-fruit systems and supports data reuse in food powder engineering, sensory science, multivariate statistics, and sustainable valorisation of agro-industrial by-products.

evidence_items.summary: This repository contains the processed 35-run modelling dataset and MATLAB R2024b code for endpoint sewing-needle temperature estimation from eight woven-fabric descriptors. The dataset comprises seven fabric profiles, each represented by five repeated two-layer, threadless fabric-penetration trials. The experimental measurements originate from the woven-fabric study reported by Dal et al. (2014). Version 2 expresses the yarn-count predictors for cotton profiles P1, P2, T1 and T2 as resultant English cotton counts, accounting for their three-ply construction. All 35 archived temperature responses and the eight predictor definitions remain unchanged. The complete analysis was repeated using the same Bayesian-regularised ANN method, nested leave-one-fabric-out validation, baseline comparisons, fabric-cluster bootstrap procedure and applicability-domain assessment. The package includes the modelling data, replication scripts, updated outer-fold predictions and performance tables, regenerated figures, effective-parameter summaries and training records, and the final exploratory full-data ANN ensemble. Predictive performance is evaluated exclusively from outer-fold predictions; the final full-data ensemble is not used for performance estimation. The response for each run is the arithmetic mean of the final 15 logged pyrometer readings, rather than an instantaneous maximum. Complete raw temperature–time series were unavailable for this secondary analysis and are not included. Version 1 contains the earlier predictor representation and model results; Version 2 should be used to reproduce the current manuscript results.
evidence_items.title: Supplementary Data and MATLAB Code for Leakage-Controlled ANN Estimation of Sewing-Needle Temperature

evidence_items.summary: Data-driven approaches for diagnosing and predicting the health of engineering systems require sufficient training data to achieve reliable performance. However, despite its high practical relevance, the question of how much data are actually required has not yet been systematically investigated.This paper presents and evaluates two complementary approaches to answering this question. Approach I fits parametric functions to the initial segments of learning curves and extrapolates them to estimate the amount of training data required to achieve a target classification accuracy. Approach II introduces a training-free, entropy-based stopping criterion that uses the gradient of normalized entropy (GNE). The information gain from the data collected over time is monitored to determine whether further data acquisition is necessary. Both approaches are evaluated using a dataset for fault classification in rolling bearings, employing a multi-layer perceptron classifier and randomly drawn, in-distribution test sets. The results show that learning curve extrapolation enables predictions of the required amount of data and that GNE can serve as an effective online stopping rule during data acquisition due to the strong correlation between GNE and classification accuracy. The two approaches complement each other: entropy analysis can monitor the progress of data acquisition in real time without model training, while learning curve extrapolation provides quantitative estimates of the remaining data requirements for specific accuracy targets.
evidence_items.title: Estimating Sufficient Amount of Training Data for Data-Driven Fault Diagnosis

rationale: Matched: agentic~benchmarking, benchmark, evaluat, safety eval
evidence_items.summary: AI agents built on large language models can assist not only legitimate tasks but also relational manipulation. AI agents can be used to help a user maintain a deceptive identity, intensify emotional dependency, isolate a target, or prepare for later extraction. We conceptualise this risk as agentic relationship harm: workflow-level assistance that can exploit recipient vulnerability, persuasive influence, and relational power asymmetry. Existing safety evaluations and generic guardrails often treat harmfulness as a property of isolated outputs, missing role-sensitive interaction patterns. To study this, we introduce a 110-prompt benchmark with balanced attacker-and victim-side cases, a relationship-specific labelling framework, and a lightweight post-generation policy gate for local agent deployments. In our evaluation, the relationship-specific gate outperforms generic safety prompting under automated judging, with no harmful-compliance cases identified on the main benchmark or multi-turn stress test while preserving victim-side protective intervention. These results suggest that relationship harm is a distinct sociotechnical risk surface and that role-sensitive evaluation plus lightweight policy gating offers a practical path beyond generic refusal prompting.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Relationship Harm: Benchmarking and Gating Relational Manipulation in AI Agents

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains 10,000 reproducible instances of the weighted Set Covering Problem, together with solver-certified integer and linear programming solutions, deterministic greedy solutions, rational certificates, and associated metadata. For the weighted Set Covering Problem, a collection of elements and a family of available subsets are given, with a positive (integer) cost assigned to each subset. The objective is to select subsets that cover every element while minimising total cost. The dataset is intended as a benchmark resource for computational experiments in combinatorial optimisation, integer programming, linear programming relaxations, approximation algorithms, greedy heuristics, and preprocessing. It may also be useful for algorithm benchmarking and teaching in operations research and computer science. The benchmark contains four matrix dimensions: (m, n) = (24, 40), (40, 70), (60, 100), and (100, 180), where m denotes the number of elements and n denotes the number of available subsets. Ten instance families are included: sparse random, medium-density random, dense random, block-structured, geometric disk-covering, interval-covering, redundant-column, dominated-column, community-structured, and planted-cover instances. Each family contains 1,000 instances, with 250 at each dimension, giving 10,000 instances in total. For each instance, the dataset provides the exact sparse incidence matrix and integer costs, optimal IP and LP objective values and corresponding solution vectors, integrality gaps, two deterministic greedy solutions, generation seed and parameters, structural statistics, solver settings, runtimes, and supporting bounds and certificates. Every instance is feasible and has solver-certified IP and LP optima. The reference optimisation experiments used AMPL with Gurobi for integer optimisation and HiGHS for the LP relaxation and explicit dual.
evidence_items.title: Set Covering Benchmark Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.
evidence_items.title: EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents

evidence_items.summary: Static coding benchmarks are fixed at release. Over time their tasks leak into training data, and stronger agents eventually saturate them. We argue that a benchmark should instead aim to be self-scaling: its tasks and oracles are created at evaluation time, so no content exists in advance to leak, and its difficulty is set by the participating agents rather than fixed at release. We introduce SWE-Duel, an arena in which two coding agents evaluate each other over mirrored Red-Blue turns. In each turn, the Red agent works on a real repository across three context-isolated sessions. It proposes and implements a new feature with feature tests, then embeds a subtle bug in that feature along with sealed bug-triggering tests. The resulting pull request is admitted only if (1) it passes the feature tests and the repository's existing tests while failing exactly the bug tests, and (2) a fresh session of the same agent can repair the bug blind, which rules out unsolvable tasks. The Blue agent then reviews the pull request without being told a bug exists. It wins only if its revision passes all three test suites, and then the two agents swap roles. We run a tournament among 11 model-harness participants on 15 repositories in five languages for 1,500 turns. The leaders win in different ways. GPT-5.5 with Codex CLI ranks first as the strongest solver, repairing 98.3% of the defects it reviews. Claude Opus 4.8 with mini-swe-agent ranks second as the strongest task author, with a 27.3% Red win rate. Finally, within one model family, tasks written by the newest version defeat a fixed-reference solver far more often than those of older versions (42.9% vs. 4.0%), giving preliminary evidence that task difficulty scales with task authoring capability.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Duel: Towards a Self-Scaling Arena for Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: The evaluation of coding agents generally strives to be as realistic as possible. In our study, we collect 4,782 agent sessions of real software engineers in JetBrains IDEs, which we call Production Sessions. Since our subject is interactive agents, we study the sessions with at least three user messages (33% of the sample). These long sessions differ from issue-derived benchmark tasks in two ways: (i) user requests span a far wider mix of task types - questions about the project's code, planning, review, refactoring, execution - and (ii) users switch between types throughout a session. Long-session samples from three public interaction corpora exhibit markedly different Task Flows (the distributions of session lengths, task types, and type-to-type transitions), so no single interaction distribution is universally realistic: benchmarks should name a target use case and calibrate to measurements from it. We present SWE-TaskFlow, an approach for transforming any issue-derived benchmark: it preserves the verified tasks and tests while steering the interaction toward a target Task Flow through prompt splitting and verifiable repository QA, with a TaskFlow Alignment Score (TFAS) for selecting among generated trajectories. In a pilot on 700 SWE-Bench Pro tasks, solving the task sequentially in several steps approximately doubles agent cost without a stable change in resolve rate: the interaction protocol itself is an important dimension of evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Coding-Agent Benchmarks Should Match Their Users' Task Flows

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid AI adoption in education, rigorous evaluation of AI-powered educational (AIED) systems remains critically underdeveloped, particularly in second-language (L2) education, one of the most common yet least evaluated AI applications. We introduce L2-Bench, an open-source benchmark of 1,000+ task-response pairs to aid the pedagogy-led evaluation of LLM capabilities relating to language learning and assessment. Crucially, L2-Bench measures model performativity on the application of learning experience design principles rather than mere knowledge of those principles or broad learning outcomes. Our contributions include: (1) a validated taxonomy of 12 competencies and 31 subcompetencies validated by 200+ expert practitioners (task authenticity = 4.42/5.00, criteria adequacy = 4.18/5.00); (2) a rubric-based evaluation methodology that we believe can, if adapted, generalize to similar (open-ended, qualitative) disciplines; (3) an evaluation dataset that produces reliable signal about model strengths, weaknesses, and contextual robustness across diverse L2 education scenarios. We find that, among large models, Claude Opus 4.7 performs best overall (85.5%), though is marginally outperformed on several constituent tasks. We also find that performance drops notably on harder tasks (ranging from 69.9%–73.4%). L2-Bench provides education stakeholders better methods to make more informed decisions about real-world AIED adoption, use, and governance, while advancing the maturing science of AI evaluations for education.
evidence_items.title: L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education (Extended Abstract)

evidence_items.summary: Benchmark suites assess model capability on controlled tasks; large-scale conversation corpora capture naturalistic use without user feedback; and in-interface feedback mechanisms record satisfaction without task purpose. Together, they leave a critical gap in LLM evaluation: no existing infrastructure routinely links interaction trajectories to user-defined outcomes. We introduce MonitrLLM, open-source infrastructure for community-centered LLM evaluations that links full conversation transcripts to user-reported task intent and outcome assessments, treating all three as primary evaluative signals rather than optional metadata. To demonstrate the value of this approach, we conducted a two-week feasibility pilot with 26 college students using ChatGPT, collecting 206 evaluation reports with full conversation transcripts. The findings from our pilot demonstrate the value of connecting conversation trajectories with user-reported outcomes. For instance, despite reporting high average satisfaction (4.19/5) with their LLM interactions, participants also experience a substantial 23.1% failure rate on their goal tasks. We also find that multi-turn conversations are reported as failing at 2.5 times the rate of single-turn exchanges, a pattern that reframes extended interaction as a signal of difficulty rather than engagement. We conclude by discussing the value of incorporating direct user feedback with observational data for robust LLM evaluations, and the possibilities for infrastructure that enables this goal.
evidence_items.title: MonitrLLM: A Community-Centered Evaluation Infrastructure for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Sixth generation (6G) networks require intelligent and privacy-preserving solutions to handle traffic complexity, resource allocation, and security challenges. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer advanced reasoning and Federated Artificial Intelligence (FAI) enables distributed learning without directly sharing raw data, their combined application in large-scale network science remains limited. Key issues include non-IID data, decision latency, and limited robustness of centralized models. To address these challenges, this work introduces FALCON-6G (Federated AI and LLM-Oriented Cognitive Optimization in 6G Networks), a novel framework for distributed anomaly detection, traffic prediction, and adaptive resource management. Experiments conducted under federated learning settings with 50 participating clients and 200 global communication rounds on two Open RAN and four intrusion detection datasets show a 22.7% average relative improvement in throughput prediction accuracy and a 17.6% reduction in decision latency compared with FedAvg, along with up to a 23.9% relative improvement in intrusion detection F1-score over FedAvg and a 34.0% reduction in communication overhead. These results demonstrate the potential of FALCON-6G for privacy-aware 6G network optimization. The current evaluation is primarily based on benchmark datasets, and validation in live large-scale 6G/O-RAN environments remains an important direction for future work.
evidence_items.title: Enhancing network science with large language models and federated artificial intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on corpora that contain expressions of human judgment about films, books, music, and more. Yet whether LLMs systematically reproduce evaluative hierarchies remains unclear. Prior research on cultural bias in LLMs suggests competing expectations: models may mirror the popularity signals of internet texts, or may reproduce forms of prestige embedded in critical discourse. We probe this question through a study of film evaluations with eight models from four families (Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba, and Mistral), using a 200-film benchmark partitioned into critically acclaimed, commercially successful, and dual-legitimacy (critical acclaim + commercial success) films. Across 20,000 pairwise forced-choice comparisons per model analyzed with Bradley-Terry estimation, we observe a consistent critical acclaim orientation with all models: critically acclaimed yet commercially obscure films are selected over commercially successful yet critically unrecognized ones. This pattern grows with model scale within each family. In addition, nested OLS regression analyses show that evaluative orientation, public visibility, and popular reception distinctly help explain preferences. Adjusting for public visibility reverses the models' preference for dual-legitimacy films over critical acclaim-only films, while additionally accounting for popular reception attenuates much of the disadvantage of films with commercial success only. Finally, evaluative and recommendation-oriented prompt framings produce divergent rankings, suggesting that critical acclaim orientation may manifest indirectly in real-world LLM deployments.
evidence_items.title: Critical Acclaim Orientation in Large Language Models: Evidence from Film Preference Elicitation
