evidence_items.summary: Weekly cycles in cyber-threat activity are well documented, but how their timing varies with national weekends is not. Across 384 series from 192 countries, the weekly cycle is nearly universal. In the 43 countries whose weekend we individually sourced, its phase is statistically associated with the local working week. Under the dataset’s date labels, activity is lowest on each country’s own first working day (Sunday) in every Friday–Saturday-weekend country. In just over half of Saturday–Sunday countries, it is lowest one day later (Tuesday rather than Monday). This separation survives any uniform shift of the labels; the absolute weekday depends on an undocumented source timezone. Amplitude is larger under Friday–Saturday weekends (p = 0.0010). Auditing the benchmark, we also found that its ambiguous date format, read with a common parsing idiom, silently discards 59.9% of the data. A full factorial of day-of-week specification, multi-step strategy, and learner, with reimplemented baselines, rolling-origin evaluation, and Diebold–Mariano/Holm inference, shows that specification improves every stable pairing at H = 10 (factors 0.57–0.87) and wins on 190 of 192 countries. It is not sufficient: the multilayer perceptron still loses to a seven-observation moving average. No learned model significantly beats a fixed-window seasonal decomposition at either operational horizon. Accuracy here is governed by specification, not architecture.
evidence_items.title: Weekly Cyber-Threat Seasonality Varies with National Weekend Convention: A Cross-National Forecasting Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: The rapid growth in reported software vulnerabilities, combined with substantial delays in manual Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) assessment, has created a critical need for automated and interpretable vulnerability scoring tools. When vulnerabilities remain unscored for long periods, organizations face greater difficulty in prioritizing patches and mitigation actions, which can leave exploitable weaknesses insufficiently addressed during a critical exposure window. This challenge is particularly important for the CVSS Base metrics, which form the foundation for severity assessment and are essential for timely risk evaluation. This paper presents WSymBERT, a neuro-symbolic approach for predicting CVSS v3.1 Base metrics by combining contextual language representations with expert-derived symbolic guidance through a symbolic-guided weighted pooling mechanism. We evaluate WSymBERT on two benchmark datasets, achieving mean accuracies of 96.2% on NVD and 94.7% on Combine across the eight CVSS Base metrics. Across the reported evaluations, WSymBERT achieved higher observed performance than the evaluated baselines, while attribution-based analyses indicated greater emphasis on security-relevant evidence under the specified evaluation protocol.
evidence_items.title: WSymBERT: a weighted neuro-symbolic model for interpretable CVSS prediction

evidence_items.summary: Background: Electronic health records (EHRs) are central to NHS clinical practice, and the value of the data they hold depends on clinicians entering structured data. Structured data entry (SDE) is nonetheless used inconsistently, and most evidence comes from US settings documenting barriers rather than the mechanisms interventions must target. This is, to our knowledge, the first study to apply the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to SDE, to examine SDE behaviour among UK NHS doctors, and to apply corpus linguistics to clinicians' free-text accounts of EHR use. Methods: A two-part mixed-methods study was conducted at a large NHS teaching hospital in central London using the Epic EHR. Study 1 was a cross-sectional survey of non-consultant grade doctors comprising the System Usability Scale (SUS), a purpose-designed TPB questionnaire, and two open-text questions analysed using corpus linguistics. Study 2 was an Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA) of semi-structured interviews with six resident doctors. Results: Eighty-three doctors responded; 65 completed the SUS and 49 the TPB questionnaire. Mean SUS score was 62.1 (95% CI 58.3-65.9), below the benchmark of 68 and equivalent to a grade of "D". Structured features were used markedly less often than narrative notes. TPB constructs explained 56% of the variance in intention (F(3,45) = 18.95, p < .001); attitudes (p = .003) and subjective norms (p = .009) predicted intention independently, whereas perceived behavioural control did not (p = .14). Intention predicted self-reported use of problem lists, event-specific templates and standardised documents, but not narrative notes. Corpus analysis identified time pressure and interface friction as dominant barriers. IPA generated four themes: structured documentation as cognitive relief; as fragile collective infrastructure; as a practice clinicians are expected to perform but not enabled to learn; and as a format that can flatten clinical reasoning. Conclusions: Engagement with SDE is driven principally by attitudes and social norms rather than by perceived control, and the barriers clinicians describe arise from the intersection of interface design, training, team norms and institutional expectation. Interventions addressing usability alone are unlikely to succeed: sustained change requires team-level normative reinforcement, specialty-relevant training that explains both how and why, and systems that preserve space for clinical narrative. Keywords: Electronic health records; structured data entry; Theory of Planned Behaviour; System Usability Scale; Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis; corpus linguistics; clinical documentation; data quality; NHS
evidence_items.title: Understanding clinician engagement with electronic health records: a mixed-methods study of structured data entry using the Theory of Planned Behaviour

evidence_items.summary: Prescription drug brand homepages are widely used entry points for medication information in the United States, yet their usability as patient-facing digital interfaces is not well characterized. We evaluated official U.S. prescription drug brand homepages using a reproducible multidomain benchmarking approach. We conducted a cross-sectional benchmarking study of 338 official U.S. prescription drug brand homepages. A high-reach brand list was derived from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services Medicare Part D dataset and validated against the Food and Drug Administration National Drug Code Directory. Each homepage was assessed using standardized mobile lab audits, field user experience metrics where available, automated accessibility checks mapped to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 Levels A and AA, and text readability measures. Overall homepage quality was summarized using a prespecified composite benchmark. Overall homepage quality, summarized by the composite benchmark, was moderate (median Score 67.1; interquartile range [IQR] 57.4−75.3), whereas lab-based performance was often weak (median Lighthouse Performance 56; IQR 47−68). Automated accessibility findings were widespread: Level A findings had a median of 7 per homepage (IQR 3−14), and only 2.7% of homepages had no Level A findings. Among homepages with field data, visual stability was poor for 20.4%. These findings indicate a practical gap between regulating informational content and delivering that content through interfaces that are consistently fast, stable, accessible, and easy to use.
evidence_items.title: Regulated medication information, accessible web delivery? A cross-sectional evaluation of united states prescription drug brand homepages

evidence_items.summary: Plant leaf diseases significantly affect crop yield and quality, posing ongoing challenges across the agriculture sectors, including cereals, vegetables, fruits, and floriculture. In response, a wide range of machine learning (ML) techniques have been explored for effective disease detection and classification. This systematic review provides a comprehensive analysis of 102 peer-reviewed studies published between 2001 and 2024, exclusively focused on ML-based approaches for identifying plant leaf diseases. Based on the PRISMA methodology, studies were selected from four major databases and organized under eight research questions (RQs), covering the end-to-end ML pipeline. The review investigates key components such as dataset collection methods, model architectures, evaluation strategies, and comparative model performance. It further analyzes the distribution of studies by plant type, disease category, and publication source. Special emphasis is placed on dataset characteristics, model generalization across domains, and challenges in real-world implementation. The review also highlights performance metrics, cross-validation strategies, and the need for scalable, explainable, and lightweight models. Gaps in the literature—such as limited availability of high-quality datasets, lack of standard benchmarking, and poor model transferability—are identified to guide future research. This focused review offers a structured, comparative overview of ML-driven leaf disease classification efforts and serves as a roadmap for researchers and practitioners aiming to enhance agricultural productivity through intelligent, data-driven plant health diagnostics.
evidence_items.title: Systematic review of machine learning models for plant and leaf disease detection and classification

evidence_items.summary: This study asks whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based models produce more accurate one-year-ahead GDP-growth forecasts than conventional econometric benchmarks, and whether climate-related information improves them. Using a balanced panel of 38 OECD economies over 1995–2023 (N = 1,102) built from World Bank national accounts, International Energy Agency renewable-energy data, Copernicus/ERA5 country-level temperature anomalies and EM-DAT disaster records, we compare a per-country AR(1) benchmark, a random walk, a Fixed Effects panel regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, Gradient Boosting and an equal-weight forecast combination. Forecasts are strictly ex ante: in an expanding-window rolling-origin design over 2010–2023, every predictor enters with a one-year lag, all preprocessing and hyperparameter tuning are nested inside each training window, and forecasts are evaluated against realised, un-winsorised growth. Accuracy differences are tested with a Diebold–Mariano test that is robust to cross-sectional dependence, complemented by block-bootstrap confidence intervals. Random Forest (RMSE = 3.35) and Fixed Effects (3.38) reduce RMSE by about 8–9% relative to the AR(1) benchmark (3.67), but no individual model is statistically superior to it. The forecast combination is the most accurate approach (RMSE = 3.23; 12.0% below AR(1); two-sided p = 0.09; 95% bootstrap interval of the loss differential excluding zero). Climate variables account for about one-third of mean absolute SHAP importance, mainly through temperature anomaly and renewable share, yet a feature-set ablation shows that they add no out-of-sample accuracy: macro-only specifications forecast at least as well. Ex-ante climate-uncertainty proxies are not associated with larger forecast errors across countries, and only one proxy shows a positive within-country association.
evidence_items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Macroeconomic Forecasting with Climate-Related Information? A Leakage-Free Out-of-Sample Evaluation for OECD Countries

evidence_items.summary: Preprint. Submitted to the International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications (IJACSA); not peer reviewed. Code and registered runs: https://github.com/ibrahimjamadi98/GAINER   Cross-encoder re-rankers are among the most effective components of retrieval and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, but they pass every candidate through every Transformer layer. This study investigates where, under a fixed compute budget, the next block of layers improves the final ranking most, and proposes Gain-Aware Allocation for Neural Re-ranking (GAINER). At each intermediate checkpoint, GAINER orders the active candidates by the expected gain in nDCG@10 from advancing them, using small rankers trained on counterfactual gains in the states the cascade actually visits, and an exact-budget schedule decides how many advance. A leak test guarantees that every decision uses only computation already paid for. In a leave-one-dataset-out evaluation on seven BEIR datasets with two backbones and five seeds, with hypotheses pre-registered before the final runs, GAINER retains 96.5% of full-depth nDCG@10 at half of the candidate-layer compute of Ettin-68M, a measured 1.69x GPU speedup. At this budget it improves on a score-based cascade by +0.0178 nDCG@10 (95% CI [0.0125, 0.0233]) and on SEE, a recent similarity-based early-exit method, by +0.0154; at a quarter of the compute, its advantage over the cascade grows to +0.063 (18% relative). Two further pre-registered hypotheses, sharing one budget across queries and replacing the learned ranker with an explicit, label-free value-of-computation rule, are not supported: intermediate-layer uncertainty barely identifies which candidates are mis-scored, so the value of further computation has to be learned.
evidence_items.title: GAINER: Gain-Aware Allocation of Transformer Depth for Efficient Cross-Encoder Re-Ranking

evidence_items.summary: The choice of optimization algorithm affects not only training time and final performance but also the reliability of the training process. While optimizers are commonly compared using accuracy and computational cost, their behavior under changes in problem conditioning and scale is less often considered together. This paper compares Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), Momentum SGD, Adam, and L-BFGS using controlled synthetic linear regression problems. The experiments independently varied sample size, feature dimensionality, condition number, and learning rate. Three sample sizes (1,000, 10,000, and 100,000), three feature dimensionalities (10, 100, and 1,000), three condition numbers (10, 100, and 10,000), and three learning rates (0.001, 0.01, and 0.1) were tested, giving a total of 324 experimental runs. Optimizer behavior was evaluated primarily through failure-to-converge rate, with loss oscillation and wall-clock runtime used as additional measures. Within the tested ranges, conditioning had a much stronger effect on convergence stability than sample size. SGD and Momentum SGD had overall divergence rates of 50.6% and 45.7%, respectively, and both diverged in every run at a condition number of 10,000. Adam had an overall divergence rate of 9.9%, increasing to 29.6% under the most severe conditioning. L-BFGS recorded the lowest overall divergence rate at 3.7% and an 11.1% divergence rate at a condition number of 10,000, but required substantially more computation time per run. The results indicate a trade-off between computational cost and convergence reliability. Under the conditions examined here, first-order methods were computationally cheaper, while L-BFGS provided greater stability as conditioning became severe. The findings also suggest that problem conditioning can be a more useful indicator of convergence difficulty than dataset size alone when comparing these optimization methods.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying the Stability–Scalability Trade-off of First-Order and Quasi-Newton Optimization Methods under Controlled Conditioning

evidence_items.summary: This dataset contains 1,683 field-collected cattle images spanning four classes: Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD, n=247), Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD, n=476), and their respective healthy controls (Healthy-FMD, n=268; Healthy-LSD, n=692). Images were compiled from real farm conditions in the fields of Cumilla, Bangladesh, between June 26 and December 11, 2025. Images were captured by field technicians using personal smartphone cameras and compiled via WhatsApp, reflecting the unconstrained, full-frame visual conditions of real veterinary fieldwork rather than curated clinical photography. The dataset is intended to support both single-disease detection and FMD-LSD differential diagnosis, a comparatively underexplored task since the two diseases can present similarly on cattle muzzles. Class Composition FMD: 247 images, median resolution 1200x1440, average file size 341.4 KB, total size 82.35 MB LSD: 476 images, median resolution 1280x1200, average file size 339.2 KB, total size 157.69 MB Healthy-FMD: 268 images, median resolution 687x632, average file size 126.1 KB, total size 33.01 MB Healthy-LSD: 692 images, median resolution 1600x1388, average file size 258.7 KB, total size 174.82 MB Total: 1,683 images, 447.87 MB Collection Method Images were captured in the field during routine examination of symptomatic and healthy cattle across farms in Cumilla, Bangladesh, over a collection period of June 26 to December 11, 2025. Photographs were taken by field technicians using personal smartphone cameras under natural farm lighting and conditions, without staging, cropping, or controlled backgrounds, and shared via WhatsApp for compilation into this dataset. The resulting full-frame images may include handler's hands, gloves, restraint equipment, and variable backgrounds, reflecting the conditions a deployable field-screening tool would actually encounter rather than idealized clinical photography.

evidence_items.summary: The burgeoning field of Large Language Models (LLMs), exemplified by sophisticated models like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, represents a significant advancement in artificial intelligence. These models, however, bring forth substantial challenges in high consumption of computational, memory, energy, and financial resources, especially in environments with limited resource capabilities. This survey aims to systematically address these challenges by reviewing a broad spectrum of techniques designed to enhance the resource efficiency of LLMs. We categorize methods based on their optimization focus—covering computational, memory, energy, financial, and network resources—and their applicability across various stages of an LLM’s lifecycle, including architecture design, pre-training, fine-tuning, and system design. Additionally, the survey introduces a nuanced categorization of resource efficiency techniques by their specific resource types, which uncovers the intricate relationships and mappings between various resources and corresponding optimization techniques. A standardized set of evaluation metrics and datasets is also presented to facilitate consistent and fair comparisons across different models and techniques. By offering a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art and identifying open research avenues, this survey serves as a foundational reference for researchers and practitioners, aiding them in developing more sustainable and efficient LLMs in a rapidly evolving landscape. To make the field more accessible to interested beginners, we not only make a systematic review of existing works and a highly structured taxonomy of resource-efficient LLMs but also release a website including a constantly-updated article list https://github.com/tiingweii-shii/Awesome-Resource-Efficient-LLM-Papers.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Efficiency: A Systematic Survey of Resource-Efficient Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Classifying Autonomous Systems (ASes) by the business sectors of their operating organizations, also referred to as AS business classification, is a relatively recent but increasingly important area of study. However, the only publicly available dataset for this purpose suffers from significant inaccuracies and limited maintainability due to its heavy reliance on third-party sources. We argue that an organization's web presence—particularly its official website—serves as a more reliable and transparent source for business classification, offering broad coverage and regularly updated information. We introduce AS2Biz, a web presence-based methodology for AS business classification. AS2Biz first constructs an AS-to-website mapping dataset, achieving 98.5% coverage and 94.4% accuracy, and then mainly leverages large language models to classify textual website content into business categories. The entire methodology is highly automated and cost-efficient. Our final AS2Biz dataset covers 94.3% of ASes and, on a 220-AS ground truth benchmark, achieves substantially higher accuracy—more than doubling the F1 score on subdivided business categories (0.78 vs 0.37) and improving the F1 score on general business sectors (0.87 vs 0.62).
evidence_items.title: AS2Biz: Leveraging Web Presence and AI to Improve AS Business Classification

evidence_items.summary: Bimetallic platinum-based alloys often exhibit superior activity compared to the benchmark pure platinum catalyst for the oxygen reduction reaction. Nevertheless, their durability remains a key challenge. The degradation of Pt-based alloy catalysts involves an interplay between compositional, structural and electrochemical changes. Resolving how these processes develop over time is essential for understanding the origin of alloy-dependent stability. Here, Pt3M (M = Cu, Ni, Co) thin-film model catalyst layers prepared by magnetron co-sputtering with uniform stoichiometry, thickness and morphology are investigated using accelerated degradation testing (ADT) and time- and potential-resolved scanning flow cell inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (SFC-ICP-MS). ADT reveals pronounced differences in the behaviour of the alloys during potentiodynamic cycling, manifested in their distinct activation behaviour and long-term stability. Pt3Cu activates most slowly but exhibits the smallest surface-area loss during extended cycling, whereas Pt3Co and Pt3Ni activate rapidly and undergo more severe degradation. On-line SFC-ICP-MS shows that this divergence emerges already during the initial contact with the electrolyte, where Pt3Co and Pt3Ni lose a significant amount of their initial Co and Ni loading, while Cu dissolution from Pt3Cu is negligible. During subsequent cycling, however, Cu dissolution ultimately exceeds the cumulative alloying-element loss of Pt3Co and Pt3Ni. Long-term stability therefore depends not only on the extent of alloying-element loss but also on when that loss occurs, identifying initial electrolyte exposure as a critical stage in Pt-alloy evolution that dictates its activation and degradation.
evidence_items.title: Dataset of "Tracing the degradation of Pt3M (M=Cu, Ni, Co) ORR catalysts: From electrolyte contact to extended cycling"

evidence_items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23335998 . Thank you for this paper. You build CRBugBench from human-verified bugs mined from repository history and traced back to the pull request that introduced them, 1,000 tasks from 98 open-source GitHub repositories plus 800 tasks from two proprietary industry repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). The agent reviews the change in a sandbox without being told a bug exists, and three LLM judges match its self-ranked findings to the known bug (Section 3.3). The best configuration, claude-opus-5 with copilot-cli, catches 71.9% of bugs in its top-5 findings, up from 47.7% for opus-4.6, and performance drops by up to 25.5% on the proprietary repositories (Section 4.3). I liked that ground truth comes from bugs humans confirmed and fixed, and that you report the combined result: 50% for humans alone, 71.9% for the best agent, 82.1% together. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. Four comments. 1. On reading versus running - In Section 4.5 you show that reading and searching take 75% of turns, while running code takes about 8%. claude-opus-5 executes code in 9.7% of turns and gpt-5.6-sol in 6.9%. You also describe the overtrust cases: in the Selenium task all models endorsed the buggy condition because the in-code comment and the PR description asserted the intended behavior, and in the Elasticsearch task opus-5 cited the defective line as its standard of correctness. In my practice, a check the agent can run is the only signal other than "looks done", and the agent sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. Could you split recall@5 by whether the trajectory contained at least one Execute action, per model? And were findings that say the code was run more often correct? 2.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract A persistent gap separates academic research priorities from the operational challenges faced by manufacturing firms. Established identification methods, among them Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) workshops, Lean audits and consultant engagements, are episodic, bounded by participant expertise and organised along departmental lines, which makes cross-departmental issues hard to surface. Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) have meanwhile shown collaborative problem-solving ability in software engineering and, more recently, in shopfloor scheduling and supply chain coordination. This article is a Perspective. It develops a framework and a research agenda; implementation and empirical evaluation fall outside its scope and are set out as its first research priorities. Three contributions are offered. The first is a synthesis of literature from industrial problem identification, LLM-based autonomous agents and manufacturing AI, which positions the proposal against existing industrial LLM agent work. The second is a framework in which six domain-specialised agents (production, quality, maintenance, supply chain, safety, energy) would collaborate through a five-phase protocol: worker-driven discovery, cross-departmental analysis, candidate-relationship detection, consensus-based financial assessment and debate-driven prioritisation. The prioritisation procedure is fully specified, including the normalisation of financial estimates, a measure of estimate dispersion, the derivation of criteria weights, a non-compensatory gate for safety-critical items and a mandatory human verification step. The third is a worked calculation on a hypothetical steel manufacturing vignette, included so that the procedure can be reproduced and scrutinised rather than as evidence of effectiveness. A preliminary qualitative readiness assessment and a three-horizon agenda of fourteen research questions complete the paper.
evidence_items.title: Large language model multiagent systems for industrial problem discovery and prioritization

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision-support systems because of their ability to interpret complex queries, synthesize information, and generate contextually relevant responses. However, their use in reliability sensitive settings remains challenging because LLMs can produce incorrect or unsupported outputs while expressing a high degree of linguistic confidence. This paper presents a confidence aware explainable AI framework for improving the reliability of LLM-based decision support. The proposed approach combines model confidence, semantic consistency across multiple stochastic generations, and explanation support to construct a composite reliability score. A selective decision module then uses this score to determine whether a generated response should be accepted, flagged for review, or withheld through abstention. The framework is evaluated across factual, commonsense, and multi-step reasoning tasks using multiple open-weight LLMs. Performance is assessed in terms of answer accuracy, expected calibration error, failure-detection AUROC, selective accuracy, and response coverage. The evaluation investigates whether combining complementary reliability signals provides a more informative assessment of response correctness than self-reported confidence, model confidence, or semantic consistency alone. The proposed framework provides a practical reliability layer for LLM-based decision-support systems by jointly communicating confidence, explanation support, and an actionable response decision, thereby helping distinguish sufficiently reliable outputs from those requiring further verification or abstention.
evidence_items.title: Confidence-Aware Explainable AI for Reliable Large Language Model Decision Support

evidence_items.summary: Purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) can be helpful for literature search and summarization but retracted articles can confuse them. It is therefore important to know how aware LLMs are of retractions. Design/methodology/approach Three open-weight (offline) LLMs were asked whether 161 high-profile retracted articles had been retracted, with a similar check for a benchmark multidisciplinary set of 34,070 non-retracted articles. Findings From titles and abstracts, in over 80% of cases the LLMs claimed that a retracted article had not been retracted (GPT OSS 120 B: 82%; Gemma 3 27 B: 84%; DeepSeek R1 72 B: 88%). Reasons for a correct retraction declaration were often wrong. For the benchmark test, there were only 55 false retraction claims from 34,070 non-retracted full-text articles, and 28 false claims when only the title and abstract were entered, suggesting that there is only a small chance that LLMs discount valid studies. When retractions are erroneously claimed, this does not seem to be due to mistakes in the article. Originality/value The results confirm for the first time that offline LLMs have little ability to distinguish between valid and retracted studies, unless they are allowed to, and do, check online. The results therefore give new evidence, based on LLM knowledge of retractions, to be cautious about LLM claims about academic findings.
evidence_items.title: Do large language models know which published articles have been retracted?

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in education, but evidence on their performance comes mainly from high-resource languages. We evaluated five commercial LLMs in Kazakh in a zero-shot setting: sentiment classification on 300 class-balanced KazSAnDRA reviews and question answering (QA) on the same 300 randomly sampled KazQAD questions with and without the gold supporting passage. Exact McNemar tests with Holm correction found no significant pairwise differences on sentiment classification, one with supporting context, and nine without context under the Containment criterion. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the higher-tier model had a larger advantage over its lower-tier counterpart when the supporting passage was removed (tier-by-regime interaction: OR = 1.92, 95% CI [1.52, 2.43]). Closed-book scores were affected by output format, inflectional morphology, and answer length. Human evaluation of 500 QA responses showed that string-based metrics substantially underestimated closed-book accuracy (0.55 by human judgement versus 0.26 by Containment). Under human judgement, the three higher-scoring models did not differ significantly from one another. Access to a relevant passage narrowed differences between models, although this oracle-context condition did not test a retrieval system. These findings support task-specific evaluation of Kazakh-language educational assistants and the use of answer-matching criteria checked against human judgement.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Kazakh-Language Educational Assistants: Sentiment Classification and Question Answering with and Without Context

evidence_items.summary: The objective of this chapter is to determine the implications of Artificial Intelligence in doctoral education to integrate it as a priority form of literacy at this educational level. In the case of doctoral education, the integration of AI is the main challenge because these future researchers will be the generators of scientific and technological knowledge who will face the challenges of an AI-influenced world. The chapter is structured in three parts. The first presents a theoretical framework focused on the characteristics of doctoral training in universities, mentioning its relevance and the different types of doctorates (research-oriented and professional). The second part discusses the concepts and dimensions of artificial intelligence literacy through an organized review of articles. The third part addresses doctoral training in the context of AI, specifically the proposed conceptual model based on student acceptance and evaluation, institutional policies, and hybrid writing-AI process.
evidence_items.title: Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education

evidence_items.summary: Educators and researchers increasingly recognize the importance of Artificial Intelligence literacy. Despite the growing body of related literature, the challenges and enabling factors for its integration into preschool education remain insufficiently explored and theoretically documented. It is crucial to understand both the difficulties and the conditions that influence its promotion, as well as the perceptions formed in kindergartens, so that these can become subjects of further investigation and evaluation. The present study aims to capture teachers’ views on the importance of Artificial Intelligence literacy in preschool education, as well as to highlight the challenges and factors that influence its implementation. The data were collected from 97 educators through a structured digital questionnaire.
evidence_items.title: Kindergarten teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence in early childhood education.

evidence_items.summary: (1) Background: The aim of this study was to analyze how teacher trainees and teachers relate to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education across socio-emotional, attitudinal, competency-based, and ethical dimensions, considering the influence of personal, academic, and professional variables. The study was conceptually framed by the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers (AI CFT), complemented by DigCompEdu as a broader reference for teacher digital competence. (2) Methods: A quantitative, non-experimental, descriptive, cross-sectional design was developed with a sample of 1292 participants from Andalusia, consisting mainly of university students, along with teachers. The ACISE-IA scale, consisting of 39 items developed by Serrano-García et al. (2026), was used for data collection. (3) Results: The results showed that age and teaching experience are negatively associated with favorable attitudes and digital competence, while academic performance is positively related to greater openness, critical reflection, and perception of competence. Likewise, significant differences were identified according to the branch of knowledge, employment status, and academic year, with more positive assessments among students and in social science areas. (4) Conclusions: Overall, the findings show that the relationship with AI is not homogeneous, but rather modulated by educational and professional trajectories, underscoring the need to design flexible teacher training models that integrate technological development with pedagogical, emotional, and ethical reflection. These findings also contribute to educational sustainability by highlighting the importance of developing teacher training strategies that support the responsible and sustained integration of AI into educational systems.
evidence_items.title: Personal and Academic Factors in Teachers’ Perceptions of Educational Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Spaceflight instruments must undergo electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) testing under strict contamination-control requirements. In this context, local RF-transparent protective covers may be considered when the test facility cannot provide the required cleanliness conditions around the hardware. This work presents an application-oriented electromagnetic assessment of candidate RF-transparent protective covers for contamination-sensitive EMC testing. Several candidate materials are characterized using the open-ended coaxial probe (OECP) technique over the 2–20 GHz band to determine their effective dielectric properties and estimate their normal-incidence flat-wall transmission coefficients. Full-cover transfer-function (TF) measurements are then performed at INTA’s BIANCHA free-space anechoic facility over the 4.5–8 GHz band, using two receiving antennas with complementary radiation characteristics: a pyramidal horn and a top-hat bicone. Hemispherical covers fabricated with five candidate materials are first assessed, including repeatability and time-domain gating analyses. An alternative cubic cover is then evaluated to study the influence of cover geometry, angular incidence and edge/corner effects. An additional S 11 based mismatch assessment is also performed to distinguish antenna input-matching effects from broader system-level antenna–cover interactions. The results show that low-loss dielectric covers can introduce limited TF perturbations within the tested free-space configuration, while also demonstrating that cover geometry has a significant impact on the angular stability of the measured response. The conclusions are therefore restricted to the experimentally validated 4.5–8 GHz BIANCHA configuration.
evidence_items.title: Electromagnetic assessment of RF-transparent protective covers for contamination-sensitive EMC testing

evidence_items.summary: Utilising language models (LLMs) to prepare STEM activities can reduce lesson-planning time, but speed does not ensure quality. A standalone model may introduce factual errors or misconceptions, use language unsuitable for children's age, or suggest unsafe materials. This paper presents a theoretical and methodological framework that treats AI as an agentic system. Models with distinct roles cross-check one another and ground their work through RAG in an expert-reviewed, curated knowledge base. The knowledge base is locally owned and human-readable, with each note recording its source and review status. The system may use local models or privacy-protecting, low-cost services. It is paired with a TPACK-based professional development programme. Prompting matters, but teachers remain responsible for evaluating the evidence and deciding whether a draft suits their context. Four conditions are proposed: ordinary generation, RAG, matched self-review, and a reviewer-agent workflow. The framework has been partially implemented as an operational alpha but has not yet been formally evaluated.

evidence_items.summary:
This study investigates how citizens perceive and discuss artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled public services, focusing on “Julia,” the AI-based chatbot launched by the Municipality of Rome. It examines online discussions, revealing sociotechnical tensions and discussing their implications for institutional legitimacy and public value in the context of local government digital transformation (DT).
 
 
 
 The study adopts a qualitative approach based on the analysis of 610 citizen comments posted across the social media platforms of the Municipality of Rome and the Mayor. A thematic analysis was conducted to identify recurring patterns in how citizens interpret and evaluate the chatbot's introduction. An engagement analysis contextualized public interactions with chatbot-related posts across platforms.
 
 
 
 The findings show that citizens interpret the chatbot not merely as a technological tool but as a symbolic representation of the public entity. Four main thematic dimensions emerged: (1) trust and mistrust toward institutions, (2) digital innovation and AI, (3) evaluation of public services and urban management and (4) political, economic and symbolic evaluations of the administration. These dimensions reflect the sociotechnical tensions associated with AI-enabled public services discussed in the literature.
 
 
 
 This study contributes to the literature on local government DT examining how citizens perceive AI-enabled public services and the associated dynamics through a critical dialogic accountability perspective.
evidence_items.title: Citizens' perceptions of AI-enabled public services: a thematic analysis of “Julia”, the chatbot of the Rome Municipality

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES
This systematic review (SR) provides updated evidence-based conclusions regarding the use of pharmacologic migraine prevention in adults to inform a new joint American Academy of Neurology (AAN) and American Headache Society practice guideline.


METHODS
A multidisciplinary panel conducted an SR following the 2017 AAN Clinical Practice Guideline Process Manual. Randomized controlled trials evaluating pharmacologic preventive treatments for adults with episodic or chronic migraine were included. Searches encompassed MEDLINE, Embase, and ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception through June 6, 2024. Studies were screened in duplicate, with dual independent risk-of-bias assessment. Outcomes included change in monthly headache days, ≥50% responder rate, and validated patient-reported quality of life (QOL) measures. Raw mean differences, standardized mean differences, and risk ratios were calculated. A modified Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation process was used to classify certainty of evidence.


RESULTS
A total of 217 studies met inclusion criteria. For episodic migraine, high-confidence evidence showed that galcanezumab and erenumab are more effective than placebo in reducing headache frequency. Moderate-confidence evidence supported benefit from atogepant, eptinezumab, fremanezumab, propranolol, topiramate, and valproate. Several additional oral agents including amitriptyline, bisoprolol, flunarizine, fluoxetine, levetiracetam, metoprolol, nifedipine, pizotifen, and telmisartan had low-confidence evidence suggesting possible benefit. For chronic migraine, high-confidence evidence supported reductions in headache frequency with fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and onabotulinumtoxinA. Moderate-confidence evidence supported benefit from atogepant, eptinezumab, erenumab, topiramate and valproate. Across both episodic and chronic migraine populations, erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab, rimegepant, atogepant, topiramate and onabotulinumtoxinA demonstrated improvements in patient-reported QOL outcomes on validated instruments. Evidence comparing active treatments was limited and generally of low or very low confidence, restricting conclusions about comparative effectiveness.


DISCUSSION
This SR provides a comprehensive synthesis of evidence on pharmacologic migraine prevention in adults. High- and moderate-confidence findings confirm the efficacy of several established and newer preventive therapies and demonstrate improvements in patient-reported outcomes across multiple validated measures. These conclusions informed the development of evidence-based recommendations, presented in a companion publication, to guide clinicians in selecting preventive medications for adults with episodic and chronic migraine.
evidence_items.title: Systematic Review of Pharmacologic Treatment for Migraine Prevention in Adults: Report of the AAN Guidelines Subcommittee and the American Headache Society.

evidence_items.summary: Speech anonymization is evaluated with automatic speaker verification attackers whose performance depends on the attribute distribution of both their training and evaluation data, which may bias privacy estimates for some speaker groups. To alleviate this issue, we introduce VoxAnon, a dataset built from VoxCeleb1 and 2 with training and evaluation splits balanced across gender, age, accent, and pitch. We extract and cross-check attributes using two complementary methods, balance trial lists per subgroup, and draw test/enrollment utterances from distinct video sources in order to limit linguistic and session bias. Comparing VoxAnon with unbalanced training and test data across four attackers and three anonymizers, we show that attribute imbalance changes which subgroups appear hardest to re-identify, in directions that depend on the attribute. In the balanced setting, residual disparities persist, mostly tied to accent and pitch, and depend on the anonymizer/attacker pair. Code and trial lists are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: VoxAnon: A balanced dataset for a fair evaluation of speech anonymization

evidence_items.summary: The growing popularity of large language models (LLMs) over the last five years has produced a large amount of technical documentation and research that are published almost exclusively in English. For low-resource languages such as Bulgarian this creates a twofold gap: a lack of accessible, systematic descriptions of the LLMs in Bulgarian, and a lack of an agreed terminology for the fundamental technical concepts. These gaps impede AI literacy, regulatory compliance under the EU AI-related legislation, and hinder the explainability and understanding of AI concepts by the wider public in general. This paper presents an integrated resource that aims to make the first steps towards addressing these gaps for Bulgarian. The first component is a structured database of LLM descriptions (currently, 424 from more than 30 families), covering open-weight, proprietary, and Bulgarian, Slavic and Balkan oriented models. The description is organised in a Neo4j graph database with information on architecture, training data, training methods, benchmarks, licensing, access conditions. The second component is a bilingual English–Bulgarian terminology dictionary of LLM-related concepts (currently comprising 251 verified entries, of which 94 attested in Bulgarian, and 157 newly proposed) across nine thematic domains. The two components are linked as descriptive nodes in the graph of LLM descriptions carry Bulgarian labels drawn from the dictionary, and any revision of terminology propagates through the database. The resources are released under CC-BY-4.0 license with a web interface in Bulgarian for search and filtering of LLMs. The intended use of the resources is to support research, education, and public engagement with AI in Bulgaria.
evidence_items.title: System for Describing Large Language Models in Bulgarian

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucination and knowledge staleness in large language models (LLMs) by injecting external knowledge into the context window, yet its effectiveness is rigidly constrained by attention dilution and inference cost. Existing knowledge-graph-enhanced methods follow a sequential “retrieve-then-compress” paradigm in which retrieval and compression are optimized independently, preventing the compressor from rectifying redundancy and noise introduced during retrieval and making it difficult to achieve globally efficient information allocation under a limited token budget. To address this paradigm-level limitation, we propose LOKG (LLM-Oriented Knowledge Graph), a high-information-density knowledge graph retrieval augmentation framework that uses token-level information density maximization as a shared design objective across schema compression, subgraph retrieval, and triple encoding. LOKG comprises three synergistic modules: Semantic Compression of Ontology Schema (SCOS) offline merges semantically overlapping relations by fusing normalized mutual information, Jaccard co-occurrence, and TransE embedding similarity under a conditional-entropy-based adaptive threshold; Topology-Aware Indexing and Multi-granularity Retrieval (TAIMR) computes topology-aware multi-hop path scores using relation-aware graph attention and node information gain, then applies late query–answer semantic re-ranking in the E5 space; Information-Theoretic Triple Compression (ITTC) formulates granularity assignment as a multiple-choice knapsack problem, adaptively allocating compact, balanced, or verbose representations to candidate triples to maximize injected information under the budget constraint. Experiments on four KGQA evaluation settings from three benchmark families (CWQ, WebQSP, PathQuestion-2hop, and PathQuestion-3hop) demonstrate that under a single-LLM-call constraint, LOKG achieves a superior accuracy–efficiency trade-off.
evidence_items.title: High-Information-Density Knowledge Graph Retrieval Augmentation for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path planning is widely applied in fields such as Internet of Things (IoT) environmental monitoring, intelligent transportation, low-altitude logistics, and autonomous inspection. With the rapid development of UAV intelligence, natural language task planning powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) has emerged as a promising research hotspot. However, in safety-critical flight missions, LLMs suffer from issues such as unstable structured outputs, insufficient understanding of complex constraints, and unreliable responses to dangerous inputs, which can jeopardize the safety and robustness of UAV path planning. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an LLM-based hierarchical safe and robust UAV path planning framework to achieve co-optimization of natural language task understanding and deterministic path search. We design a Prompt–RAG–Validator safety enhancement mechanism that improves the LLM’s safety decision-making capabilities through prompt constraints, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and rule validation, while constructing a structured constraint representation to convert natural language requirements into parsable planning constraints. Furthermore, we combine a grid cost map with the A algorithm to achieve autonomous obstacle avoidance and safe grid-path generation. In addition, a two-stage evaluation system targeting both the constraint generation layer and the path-planning layer is constructed to verify model output reliability and actual planning performance. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method across various complex scenarios, including multi-constraint tasks, risk-zone planning, incomplete input information, and prompt injection attacks. Notably, on the current template-derived benchmark, the deterministic regex/slot parser provided a stronger baseline with no dangerous outputs, whereas the LLM-based pipeline offers greater flexibility in handling diverse linguistic expressions.
evidence_items.title: Hierarchical Safe and Robust UAV Path Planning Based on Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Structure-guided mutation design requires relating a proposed substitution to its molecular environment to anticipate its effects. Existing evaluations of large language models (LLMs) in protein engineering emphasize sequence-based prediction or tool-integrated workflows, leaving unclear whether LLMs themselves can infer mutation effects from structural evidence without dedicated predictors. We evaluate physical intuition-qualitative reasoning that connects structural observations with molecular interaction principles-using a benchmark that tests the same substitution in the same protein across different binding partners, with predictions based on local atomic coordinates and no dedicated mutation-effect predictors. In the tested comparisons, the best-performing LLM achieved group accuracy comparable to the evaluated energy predictors and Biomni, an LLM-driven tool workflow, while the methods differed in their prediction patterns. Most evaluated LLMs achieved higher group accuracy for larger affinity improvements. Structural interventions support selective dependence on mutation-site and partner information, while assessable structural claims largely agree with the supplied coordinates. These findings support direct LLM structural reasoning as a basis for developing rational mutation-design tools that connect molecular observations with partner-specific effects.
evidence_items.title: Probing Physical Intuition in Large Language Models through Partner-Dependent Mutation Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Layout evaluation in early-stage building design often relies on manual inspection to verify compliance with spatial requirements such as adjacency, accessibility, capacity, and programme-specific constraints. As programmes grow in size and interdependency, review becomes time-consuming, inconsistent across reviewers, and difficult to integrate into rapid iteration. This paper proposes an automated method to identify and repair non-compliant spatial layouts represented as graphs, while preserving interpretability and limiting unnecessary changes to designer intent. A candidate layout is encoded as an attributed, weighted graph, and requirements are formalised as a target benchmark graph specifying expected spaces, relations, and admissible attribute ranges. Structured compliance checking aligns candidate and benchmark graphs to detect structural violations, including missing or redundant spaces and incomplete connectivity, and attribute violations, including incorrect capacities, distances, edge weights, or constraint-relevant labels. The method then applies modular repair operators, including node insertion or deletion, edge completion, weight correction, and constraint-aware attribute adjustment, to produce a revised graph with improved benchmark conformity. Each edit is logged with its triggering violation, the operation applied, and the resulting change in compliance metrics, enabling transparent auditing and traceability. Experiments across multiple scenarios and benchmark configurations show consistent gains after repair, reducing detected violations and increasing overall benchmark alignment. The resulting logs provide actionable evidence for automated pipelines and human review, positioning graph repair as a practical quality-assurance layer for compliance-oriented generative layout workflows. Future work will scale to larger and noisier benchmarks and incorporate designer preferences and multi-objective trade-offs.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark-Guided Graph Repair for Compliance-Oriented Spatial Layout Networks

In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of computer vision based 3D anomaly detection techniques from the perspectives of multimodal 3D-AD, point cloud 3D-AD, pose-agnostic 3D-AD, dataset, and benchmarks. In addi- tion, we highlight several inherent or emerging challenges in 3D anomaly detection. The advantages and disadvantages of representative network archi- tectures for different tasks are discussed. Finally, we summarize the research results and point out future research directions. evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Machine-learning studies of autism spectrum disorder from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging routinely report near-perfect accuracy, yet the models rarely transfer to an unseen scanner. We audited a pipeline of the kind this literature builds, which reported an accuracy of 0.999, and traced that number to five data-leakage pathways. Methods: Under a nested leave-one-site-out protocol on 871 participants from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange, in which the held-out site influenced nothing but model selection, the threshold, the combiner, or the site correction, we closed every pathway, priced each by reopening it, and validated on a locked external cohort. Results: With all five pathways closed, the graph attention network reached an area under the curve of 0.648 and did not outperform a support vector machine on the same connectivity (0.679; p = 0.009). Decision-level fusion added nothing detectable (0.682, p = 0.72). A network identified its training participants better than it detected autism (0.710 versus 0.610); both questionnaire benchmarks proved label-tautological, and performance held on the external cohort. Conclusions: Reported gains in this literature should be read as claims about evaluation protocols until shown otherwise on an untouched acquisition site; all predictions, models, and code are released.
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Benchmark for Leakage-Resistant Machine Learning on Multi-Site Brain Connectivity Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Agent frameworks expose tools, delegation, memory and human approval, yet the controls attached to a request (identity, tenant, scopes, budgets, deadlines, rate limits, fail behavior) are routinely lost at execution boundaries: delegation, threads, streaming, resume, caching, retrieval and adapter exports. We present Agent Foundry, an open-source Python platform whose architecture is organized around one principle: every control is a property of the request’s execution scope, not an argument that each layer must remember to pass. We formalize this as the Governed Execution Contract (GEC), a meet-semilattice of control scopes with seven invariants, and prove that delegation can only attenuate authority, that deny rules can only tighten resolution, that per-principal rate limits are exact under arbi-trary thread interleavings, that every call yields exactly one audited decision even when the policy source is unreachable, and that admission partitions by principal without cross-shard coordination. On AgentGovBench, a public 48-scenario gov-ernance benchmark, Agent Foundry passes 48/48 in 10 of 10 repetitions, against 46/48 for the best published governed configuration and 13/48 for each of 7 pub-lished framework-native runners; run through the same harness, Microsoft’s Agent Governance Toolkit scores at most 46/48 and Bounded Agents 36/48, and on a 24-scenario suite authored blind to our code Agent Foundry scores 24/24 against 17 and 8. A set of 13 single-control ablations attributes 35 of the 48 scenarios to specific mechanisms and exposes a measurement problem: a runner that denies every call scores 31/48, above the audit-only reference, and two controls can be re-moved without losing an official point. Eight supplemental discriminating scenar-ios and three anti-vacuity checks close that gap.
evidence_items.title: Agent Foundry: A Boundary-Preserving Architecture for Governed Agentic Platforms

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This article develops a Human Governed Agentic Project Management (HG-APM) model for integrating autonomous AI capabilities with human project management authority. Design/methodology/approach: An integrative conceptual synthesis combines four literature streams: AI-enabled project management, autonomous Manager Agents, human oversight governance, and human–AI teaming. Source supported findings are separated from conceptual inferences, and the resulting architecture is expressed as a closed-loop model. Findings: The model comprises Sense, Understand, Diagnose, Predict, Plan, Evaluate, Authorize, Act, Monitor, Learn and Replan. It proposes a consequence sensitive, graduated autonomy rather than a single autonomy level. Routine and reversible actions may be automated within predefined boundaries, whereas consequential financial, contractual, scope, safety, stakeholder, reputational and strategic decisions require stronger authority from the designated human or organizational decisionmaker. Originality: The model integrates project-management intelligence, human–AI teaming and governance into one operational architecture. It contributes to a project specific decision boundary and testable propositions for evaluating whether governed agentic AI improves project outcomes without weakening human control.
evidence_items.title: Designing A Human-Governed Agentic Project Management  Model: A Closed-Loop Architecture for Autonomous Project  Intelligence, Decision Control and Human–AI Teaming

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous firewalls rely on behavioral signals, yet conventional evaluation paradigms treat them as static classifiers. We conceptualize network defense through attacker-defender co-adaptation, in which blocking a source pushes attackers toward evasion. Modeling this as a feedback loop exposes a critical blind spot: static benchmarks elide policy-induced behavioral shifts. Extending our prior works on attackers' behavioral signatures, this perspective grounds agentic defense: resilience requires tracking persistent campaigns as they redistribute across infrastructure.
evidence_items.title: Poster: Vertex - Towards Recommender Firewalls Resilient to Post-Detection Evasion

evidence_items.summary: AI browsing agents are an emerging class of AI-driven bots capable of autonomously navigating websites. Unlike traditional web bots, AI browsing agents typically operate using real browsers and perform everyday tasks, making them difficult to detect. In this poster, we present FP-Agent, the first controlled measurement study of seven AI browsing agents and human users. To evaluate the effectiveness of existing industrial bot detection solutions, we first perform a case study, finding that only one of the seven AI browsing agents are detected. Motivated by these results, we use an instrumented honey website to collect the browser and behavioral fingerprint features produced by AI browsing agents and humans while performing three tasks modeled after common real-world interactions: flight booking, online shopping, and forum interaction. We then train a multi-class classifier to analyze the discriminative power of these fingerprint features. We find that AI browsing agents can have identical browser fingerprints with each other and with humans. Behavioral fingerprints, however, are distinctive: differences in typing, scrolling, and mouse behavior separate AI browsing agents from humans and one another, showing that they are a critical component to reliably detect and control this emerging form of web traffic.
evidence_items.title: Poster: FP-Agent: Towards Fingerprinting AI Browsing Agents

evidence_items.summary: PLANETARY AND EXTREME-ENVIRONMENT QUANTUM–NANO OBSERVATORY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance This exploratory research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for quantum-enabled and classical sensor networks operating in extreme terrestrial and possible off-world environments. It asks how a distributed observatory can remain scientifically useful under contact loss, power scarcity, reference aging, thermal and radiation stress, material degradation, ambiguous physical changes, delayed commands and difficult maintenance. The central criterion is not uninterrupted telemetry but defensible measurement meaning: a raw observation must retain its measurand, units, calibration lineage, time context, uncertainty and revision history or be declared untrustworthy. The work combines three mother research architectures while respecting their evidential limits. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 65–80, contributes distributed robotics, fault-tolerant task allocation, remote servicing, resource limits and field operations. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, particularly chapters 43–49 and 58–82, contributes bounded autonomy, fleet metrology, human override, classical fallback, recovery and successor handoff. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 33–56 and 79–82, contributes network fault isolation, calibration lineage, replayable evidence and common-mode drift detection. Their intersection motivates proposed experiments but does not demonstrate mature planetary quantum–nano observatories. The central three-coupling is Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance. The candidate mission-continuity heuristic R mission = R energy × R reference × R comm × R recovery × R data represents a useful checklist of necessary capabilities but is not a validated physical law.
evidence_items.title: PLANETARY AND EXTREME-ENVIRONMENT QUANTUM–NANO OBSERVATORY NETWORKS AT THE LIMIT  Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance  This exploratory research monograph develops a falsifiable architecture for quantum-enabled and classical sensor networks operating in extreme terrestrial and possible off-world environments. It asks how a distributed observatory can remain scientifically useful under contact loss, power scarcity, reference aging, thermal and radiation stress, material degradation, ambiguous physical changes, delayed commands and difficult maintenance. The central criterion is not uninterrupted telemetry but defensible measurement meaning: a raw observation must retain its measurand, units, calibration lineage, time context, uncertainty and revision history or be declared untrustworthy.  The work combines three mother research architectures while respecting their evidential limits. Swarm Manufacturing and Robotic Matter at the Limit, particularly chapters 65–80, contributes distributed robotics, fault-tolerant task allocation, remote servicing, resource limits and field operations. Autonomous Quantum Health Infrastructure at the Limit, particularly chapters 43–49 and 58–82, contributes bounded autonomy, fleet metrology, human override, classical fallback, recovery and successor handoff. Self-Calibrating Quantum Biosensing Networks at the Limit, particularly chapters 33–56 and 79–82, contributes network fault isolation, calibration lineage, replayable evidence and common-mode drift detection. Their intersection motivates proposed experiments but does not demonstrate mature planetary quantum–nano observatories.  The central three-coupling is Extreme Habitat × Distributed Sensing × Delay Tolerance. The candidate mission-continuity heuristic R_mission = R_energy × R_reference × R_comm × R_recovery × R_data represents a useful checklist of necessary capabilities but is not a validated physical law. A product of stage reliabilities requires additional independence assumptions. Joint mission survival must account for correlated failures, shared environmental stresses, time-varying hazard rates, depleted resources and common calibration chains. A highly sensitive quantum sensor is not necessarily preferable to a more durable classical instrument once mass, power, packaging, cryogenic or optical stabilization, calibration, data transport and lifecycle cost are included.  The monograph contains 82 research chapters with 12 individually paginated study units per chapter, 30 physical and mathematical derivation plates, a distinct candidate research model and spatial network geometry for each chapter, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each of the 233 research entrances is paired with a numbered mathematical or physical equation egg. These eggs identify known scientific relationships and interpretation boundaries; they are not newly discovered physical laws. The derivation plates are concise research derivation sketches, not complete mathematical monographs.  The experimental program proposes chamber and field-analog comparisons across thermal cycling, vibration, pressure, salinity, contamination, radiation-relevant exposure and delayed or interrupted communications. It challenges independent versus common-mode reference failures, expired calibration artifacts, clock desynchronization, partial network partitions, compromised firmware, cold starts, long no-contact intervals and station retirement. Classical-only, frozen-calibration and manual-reviewed workflows are mandatory comparators where appropriate. Bench tests, field qualification and actual lunar, Martian or deep-ocean deployments are distinct evidence levels. This volume does not claim that the integrated system is currently mission-qualified.  A 200-Gate research atlas and related spreadsheets support independent laboratories. Gate records specify questions, controlled experiments, independent acceptance and veto criteria, measurement and reference histories, source lineage, energy-data budgets, communication outage tests, fault injections, recoverability, and successor reconstruction. The 33 Answer Embryos remain provisional structures that can be rejected, separated into classical-only alternatives, repaired or reborn. Scientific retirement and no-data states are treated as legitimate results, not failures of intelligence.  SCIENTIFIC BOUNDARY. This is a large-scale, partly template-assisted hypothesis and research-design atlas, not a report of completed physical experiments, qualified space hardware, peer-reviewed validation or guaranteed quantum advantage. A high numerical consensus cannot substitute for a reliable external reference. A robust communication protocol cannot repair a lost measurand or improperly calibrated instrument. Any field deployment would require environment-specific engineering qualification, safety review, lawful mission authority, suitable environmental stewardship and independent verification. Background guidance includes BIPM/JCGM evaluation of measurement uncertainty and NASA documentation of Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking; neither validates the novel integrated platform. evidence_items.summary: As AI systems tackle increasingly open-ended research problems, human experts may struggle to assess results and guide further progress. The model itself may be the best available optimizer and evaluator. The challenge is obtaining useful self-supervision within that homogeneous loop, where a model risks reinforcing its own blind spots rather than correcting them. We ask whether a model can learn from the collective intelligence of its own team. Introducing our new paper, Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision : Detailed Blog: https://pub.sakana.ai/mass/ Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12176 Code: https://github.com/SakanaAI/mass We introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS). One shared model solves tasks through a team of virtual subagents, searches for better multi-agent workflows, then uses its own judgments to select the best ones. Training on the best team’s executions distills the team’s collective experience back into the shared model. We ran two cycles using a 27B open-weights model on synthetic open-ended research tasks. After the second cycle, score per output token reached 1.2-1.6x the base model’s level across four research benchmarks. Three key results: MASS enables role generalization within an RSI loop: training only on task-solving data from the optimizee naturally improves the capabilities of both the optimizer and the evaluator. multi-agent trajectories are more efficient training data than single-agent trajectories for RSI. optimizer capacity, rather than evaluator capacity, can be the bottleneck in the speed of improvement. We believe the community needs to investigate homogeneous RSI carefully to support AI safety. When a model is also its own evaluator, shared blind spots could allow mistakes to be accepted as progress and reinforced through training. For AI to improve beyond human expertise safely, we need to understand these failures and preserve effective ways to detect them and intervene.
evidence_items.title: Recursive Self-Improvement through Collective Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) benchmarks are not neutral tools of evaluation but socio-technical artefacts that shape competition, power, and research priorities within AI. Benchmarks standardise the assessment of systems and facilitate the creation of leaderboards that reward state-of-the-art performance with prestige, citations, trust, and institutional influence. As the costs of developing competitive AI systems rise, these rewards increasingly concentrate among powerful, industry-funded labs. This paper situates these concerns within Iris Marion Young's theories of oppression and structural injustice. It argues that current benchmarking practices may perpetuate systematic harms affecting various actors in AI research, aligning with four of Young’s "faces of oppression". Benchmarking culture is further framed as a source of structural injustice, as these harms emerge from normalised, individually defensible practices and network effects, even without explicit wrongdoing. By reinforcing existing power structures and narrowing possible research trajectories, benchmarking may in fact prevent the field from advancing in epistemically robust and socially beneficial ways.
evidence_items.title: The Benchmark Trap: Structures of Power and Injustice in AI Evaluations
