evidence_items.summary: As the production of software passes into the hands of software itself, coding agents are increasingly commissioned to build agents fitted to their users' own workflows. This delegation carries a quiet assumption, that the delivered agent will faithfully serve the requirement it was built for, rather than merely appear to. No existing benchmark tests that assumption. We introduce AgentSWE, a benchmark for agent software engineering spanning three stages of the agent development lifecycle: Creation of a complete agent from a natural-language requirement, Editing of production agent codebases, and Optimization toward a measurable target. Each of its 25 tasks is framed as a commission rather than an exam: the builder iterates against a handful of illustrative cases, while acceptance exercises the frozen submission on held-out cases designed to span the full requirement, grading behavior against requirement-derived rubrics under hard pass/fail gates or, for Optimization, against the source benchmark's own objective. Evaluating a range of coding agents across models and harnesses, we find that none comes close to delivering what a requirement asks for: the gap between what a builder demonstrates and what it delivers is the norm, not the corner case. An accompanying empirical analysis of the failure trajectories identifies recurring failure modes, among them overfitting to the visible cases, hollow runtimes behind code that looks complete, and unsupported claims of completion, each a signal by which coding agents can learn to build the agents they are asked for.
evidence_items.title: AgentSWE: Can Coding Agents Build the Agent You Actually Want?

evidence_items.summary: Terminal agents are moving beyond local operations toward completing real-world professional tasks. Short trajectories can demonstrate commands and tool calls, but they do not fully show how agents accumulate evidence through exploration, use it to inform judgments, continually adjust strategies based on feedback, and turn intermediate results into final deliverables. High-quality long-horizon trajectories capture these agentic behavioral patterns and their connections within a single problem-solving process, providing richer experience for sustained autonomous work. However, environment synthesis may complete or simplify the key work underlying these patterns in advance and thus remove the need for exploration, implementation, and verification that the agent was meant to perform. To address this, we introduce TerminalHorizon, a fully automated data synthesis engine for long-horizon terminal agents. Starting from real-world professional work, it uses independent execution to identify key work omitted during construction and uses the resulting evidence to guide environment reconstruction. To extend these patterns across stages, it progressively expands tasks under the same goal, introducing new requirements that build on prior results and call for further exploration and improvement. Using this engine, we construct 1.5K task environments and perform supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on the resulting dataset to obtain TerminalHorizon-27B. We achieve substantial performance gains on all 12 benchmarks spanning coding-agent tasks, agentic tasks in real-world production settings, and general reasoning. Multiple RSI case studies, each with a 12-hour research budget, further demonstrate the model's ability to continue experimenting beyond an initial solution, improve its methods based on feedback, and retain effective improvements in its final deliverables.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Agentic Data for Long-Horizon Terminal Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.
evidence_items.title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction

evidence_items.summary: Continual post-training faces a dual challenge of acquisition and retention: models must learn new capabilities while preserving prior knowledge. While Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) mitigates this using self-supervision with in-context demonstrations, it relies on strong in-context learning and instruction-following abilities. Consequently, SDFT fails on smaller models critical for low-latency, on-device use. To enable continual learning at smaller scales, we first identify the root cause of failure. We show that poor acquisition and forgetting correlate linearly with the post-trained model's distribution shift, revealing the necessity of in-distribution learning. We thus introduce Synthetic Self-Distillation (SynthSelf), imitating SDFT's in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger, same-family aligner. Coupled with off-policy supervision and rejection sampling, this provides the high-quality supervision small models require without breaking their original distribution. Evaluations spanning 4 acquisition datasets (including a mixture) and 14 retention benchmarks show SynthSelf consistently outperforms 6 methods (including off- and on-policy distillation) across 3 small model scales. Extensive further analyses confirm SynthSelf paves the way toward effective small-model continual learning.
evidence_items.title: Continually Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation

evidence_items.summary: Adversarial games have driven advances from heuristic search to reinforcement learning, yet learning and adapting strategies from limited samples remain challenging. AI agents offer an alternative by turning game experience into revisions of executable policies. Building on heuristic learning (HL), we formalize Adversarial Heuristic Learning (AHL), a paradigm that uses AI agents as learning engines to refine game policies and supporting software while keeping model weights fixed. We introduce AAArena, a benchmark comprising 12 authentic adversarial games and 1,920 archived human programs, with an evaluation protocol modeled on real-world game competitions. Agents interpret rules, choose opponents, analyze replays, and revise game agents to achieve their highest ranking within fixed match and evaluation budgets. We evaluate completedmodels model and harness configurations: Opus5.5 with Claude Code earns 6 gold medals, while no evaluated configuration tops the remaining 6 human ladders. Performance is generally weaker in games with more complex rule specifications. Further experiments show that opponent selection and dense feedback support policy improvement, and that agents learn from both on-policy replays of their own matches and off-policy replays of other players' matches. These results highlight HL's potential in adversarial games and identify persistent challenges in game understanding, strategy implementation, and long-horizon policy development.
evidence_items.title: Can AI Agents Learn Their Way to the Top? Evaluating Heuristic Learning in a Long-Running Game Agent Competition

evidence_items.summary: Reward modeling often requires jointly representing and reasoning over multiple evaluation criteria, yet verbalizing this process token by token can incur substantial inference cost. Recent work on latent reasoning suggests that continuous states may support this computation more compactly. We introduce LatentGRM, a latent evaluation framework built on semantic chunking, compression, and reconstruction. By using the structure of rubric-guided evaluations to guide compression, LatentGRM learns compact continuous trajectories that support autonomous pairwise judgments without generating textual assessments. A separate interpreter reconstructs evaluation text from these trajectories, providing an offline view of the information retained under compression. Under matched training data and backbones, LatentGRM achieves competitive aggregate preference accuracy relative to explicit Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) judges at both 4B and 8B scales. Across four benchmark domains, LatentGRM-8B compresses evaluation trajectories by 8.9--9.2x and reduces total judge inference time by 6.1--7.0x at vote@5. Controlled rubric interventions show that criterion-dependent preference information is carried through the latent sequence. Together, these results demonstrate that continuous latent evaluation can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving competitive judgment quality.
evidence_items.title: Judging in Latent Space: Efficient Generative Reward Modeling via Semantics-Preserving Compression

evidence_items.summary: Automated research systems increasingly run LLM agents over long horizons, but more inference does not by itself produce more progress: agents replay growing histories, duplicate one another's work, or stop experimenting while token consumption continues. Yet most evaluations use short budgets or benchmarks that saturate early, leaving these failure modes untested. We trace these failures to two choices: where research state lives and who decides what to try next. We introduce Stateless Language Agents (SLAs), built on the principle of stateful search with stateless agents: no agent carries its conversation across invocations; instead, the harness owns the research state (candidate solutions and measured outcomes) and reconstructs a fresh and role-specific context for every invocation. What each agent sees becomes an explicit design choice rather than a history that grows with the run. We implement this principle in the SLA framework, where a stateless Advisor reads harness-summarized evidence across search directions and assigns concrete experiments to parallel Workers. We evaluate SLA against three recent frameworks on software engineering, kernel optimization, and algorithm design at budgets of up to one billion tokens. SLA achieves the best final result on every task and reaches the strongest kernel baseline's final performance with over 84% fewer tokens. Ablations from shared checkpoints show that focused contexts and explicit assignments each contribute to SLA's progress, with effects that can compound over full runs, while the Advisor consumes less than 0.6% of tokens. These results argue for SLAs, which keep durable research state out of agent conversations, and show that short evaluation horizons can misjudge research systems and their components.
evidence_items.title: Stateless Language Agents: Scaling Long-Horizon Automated Research

evidence_items.summary: Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control. Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines. Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%). As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. On RoboTwin 2.0, it outperforms every mainstream backbone we evaluate in all four out-of-distribution settings, by up to 24.8% relative to the strongest backbone. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%. On nuScenes, used as the visual backbone, GroundingPI attains an average open-loop L2 error of 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Downstream autonomous driving and robotic manipulation improve as the pretraining is scaled. Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.
evidence_items.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives

evidence_items.summary: Foundation models can serve as clinical agents through tool-use harnesses. However, conventional medical benchmarks assess reasoning over preselected evidence rather than the ability to seek it across clinical records and longitudinal imaging. We propose CASE: a series of role-specific Clinical Agents for Seeking Evidence, together with a tool-use harness and an agentic post-training framework for compact vision-language policy models. We further introduce a longitudinal multimodal benchmark built on UK Biobank, comprising 50,401 clinical questions derived from real-world ICD-10-coded diagnoses of 4,739 participants. Each question links to a patient-specific environment containing clinical context and multi-sequence MRI from baseline and follow-up visits, where agents autonomously select which visits, organs, modalities, slices, and specialist tools to inspect and compare. Supervised fine-tuning transfers evidence-seeking workflows from 14,734 frontier-model interaction trajectories, followed by agentic reinforcement learning on the learner's own environment interactions. Privileged on-policy self-distillation and rubric-based LLM feedback refine evidence-to-conclusion reasoning without prescribing tool sequences. Experiments show that CASE moves beyond question-answer imitation toward transferable investigation policies, strengthening evidence-grounded longitudinal reasoning. Under matched evaluation conditions, our Qwen3-VL-8B based agent achieves over 16% and 10% relative improvements in answer accuracy over GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.8. Code will be available at https://github.com/VinyehShaw/CASE.
evidence_items.title: From Given to Gathered Evidence: Agentic Learning for Longitudinal Medical Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents can now write, run, and debug programs with little human help. Robot tasks, however, are usually specified by a sentence that leaves out how to grasp, in what order to make contact, and what the result should look like, and an agent given only the sentence must find these details by trial and error. We introduce ENCORE, which gives the agent a few demonstrations as evidence to read rather than as training data. A deterministic builder distills each demonstration into a pack of multi-view keyframes, gripper events, frame strips, and the full trajectory. A coding agent studies the pack, writes a policy program against a fixed perception and action API, refines it iteratively over a few development rollouts, and freezes it before a sealed evaluation that never reveals the success signal. On LIBERO-PRO, the agent's first program already succeeds in half of the perturbed tasks with demonstrations and in one task without them, and the frozen programs outperform the strongest prior agentic system run with the same language model (96.3% against 89.3%). On RoboDojo tasks whose instructions leave the goal unstated, no program succeeds without demonstrations. ENCORE also runs on a real bimanual robot, learning cube handover and cup inversion from five demonstrations each.
evidence_items.title: Encore: Few-Shot Agentic Discovery of Manipulation Strategies

evidence_items.summary: Process reward models (PRMs) have become a key component for LLMs, as their step-level feedback supports both post-training and test-time reasoning. However, training strong PRMs remains costly: human step annotation is difficult to scale, while Monte Carlo estimation is computationally expensive and can drift from the intrinsic correctness of steps. To get effective PRMs at low cost, we introduce TIPS (Thinking-Induced Process Supervision), an outcome-only reinforcement learning (RL) framework for training generative PRMs. In TIPS, the model generates a chain-of-thought (CoT) followed by step-level labels and an outcome label. The reward depends solely on whether the predicted outcome matches the ground truth, and the resulting group-relative advantage is used to optimize the entire generated response. Intuitively, when checking intermediate steps helps determine the outcome, more accurate checks can lead to better outcome judgments and higher rewards. Outcome-only RL can therefore reinforce step-level verification without explicit process supervision. We validate the effectiveness of TIPS across math and agent benchmarks and four backbone families. Notably, TIPS-Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 reaches 85.2 F1 on ProcessBench with only 3.2K outcome-labeled trajectories, surpassing all evaluated trained PRMs and strong prompt-only judges such as GPT-5.4-Instruct and Claude-4.7-Opus, while still trailing o1-mini. Code and data are available at https://github.com/RUCBM/TIPS.
evidence_items.title: Inducing Process Supervision from Outcome-Only Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Video understanding agents acquire evidence through an executable harness that controls what they observe and how they use those observations. However, execution traces contain only the evidence acquired by the current harness, leaving competing explanations for failure unresolved and limiting the basis for self-improvement. We introduce Video-RSI, a framework for recursive self-improvement in which a video understanding agent uses its own language model to revise its harness. Through active video investigation, the model revisits the original training videos to test competing failure explanations with additional observations, grounding proposed changes in evidence beyond the existing trace. Cost-aware harness evolution turns these diagnoses into reusable revisions and determines which revisions to retain by considering both answer accuracy and visual cost. Across our evaluation settings on video understanding benchmarks, the evolved agent improves accuracy while processing fewer frames and achieves competitive accuracy-efficiency trade-offs against existing video understanding agents. These results demonstrate the potential for video understanding agents to improve their own evidence acquisition and use through harness evolution. Code is available at https://github.com/bingjunluo/Video-RSI .
evidence_items.title: Video-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Understanding Agents via Harness Evolution

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the dataset and supplementary materials of a systematic literature review examining how artificial intelligence (AI) applications used in school education relate to students' engagement, psychological and socio-emotional well-being, and self-regulated learning (SRL), the pedagogical and psychological mechanisms through which these effects are reported to occur, and the contextual, learner-related, teacher-related and technological conditions that shape them. The review covers early childhood, primary, lower and upper secondary, vocational and special education settings; higher education was excluded by design. Records were retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC and APA PsycInfo (EBSCO) using a search string combining AI-related terms (e.g., artificial intelligence, machine learning, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring, adaptive learning, chatbots, conversational agents, generative AI, large language models), school-education and population terms, and well-being, emotional, motivational, engagement and self-regulation terms. After the application of formal filters (peer-reviewed journal articles, full-text availability, English or Italian language, publication year ≥ 2014), 4,304 records were retained; following duplicate removal, 3,624 records were screened by title and abstract, 130 full-text reports were assessed for eligibility, and 84 empirical studies were included. Screening was conducted independently by multiple reviewers, and inter-rater agreement data for both screening stages are provided. Annex A (Systematic Dataset) contains the extraction codebook, the PRISMA flow data with reasons for full-text exclusion, the bibliographic records exported from each database, the screening decisions at the first (title/abstract) and second (full-text) stages, the inter-rater agreement data, and the list of included articles.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence, student engagement, well-being and self-regulated learning in school education: Systematic review dataset and supplementary analytical materials

The persona corpus supplies broad affect-heavy conversational material; this release supplies contrastive pairs for the three defects that remained visible after SFT-style corpus work: overlong answers, mirroring the user's message length and shape, abstract, category-level language in place of concrete… See the full description on the dataset page: https://huggingface.co/datasets/OusiaResearch/Vireth-DPO-Preference-Pairs.

evidence_items.summary: Large environmental datasets are increasingly available from multiple sources. These datasets are often characterised by heterogeneous data-generating mechanisms, varying uncertainty structures, and differing spatial and temporal resolutions. This heterogeneity poses significant challenges to the production of coherent and reliable official environmental statistics, which are essential for monitoring environmental processes and informing evidence-based policy decisions. Model-based approaches provide a systematic way to integrate these complex data sources, enabling consistent estimation and uncertainty quantification.  Air quality datasets sit at the intersection of many research fields. However, building a ready-to-use data product requires solving several statistical challenges, such as harmonising heterogeneous sources, detecting outliers, imputing missing data with propagated uncertainty, and reconciling spatial supports across applications. In this work, we present the AQCLIM data product, which combines a variety of daily air quality and climate data for Italy from 2013 to 2023. Using the AQCLIM dataset, we study the change-of-support problem with a Fixed Rank Kriging (FRK) model and propose a multivariate Low-Rank State-Space Model (LR-SSM) implemented in the geossm Python package.
evidence_items.title: Geostatistical modelling of complex environmental datasets

evidence_items.summary: Objectives: Patients and clinicians increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) about Kampo, Japan's traditional medicine. Yet evaluations of LLMs have measured accuracy on examination questions, which ask what a model knows; a consultation asks whether it can apply that knowledge to the patient at hand. No benchmark had measured that. Materials and Methods: KampoBench comprises 74 consultation scenarios and 310 conversation-specific rubric criteria, following the design of HealthBench. Scenarios, criteria and reference answers were drafted by an LLM and revised by board-certified Kampo physicians. Ten current models from three vendors were evaluated. Because LLM graders are known to favor their own family, each response was graded by a model from each vendor. Results: The best model reached 74.8-86.3% across graders, the physician-revised reference answers 87.9-92.4%. Rankings were stable across graders (Spearman's rho 0.952-0.976), and the family-favoring deviation was 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points, below the bootstrap standard deviation of one measurement; grader leniency varied by 14.3 points. Models were most reliable on criteria about advising that care be sought (83.6%) and least reliable on those requiring a known crude-drug risk to be tied to the case (17.5%), though 79.2% of those responses named the drug. Discussion: The shortfall lay in applying knowledge to the case rather than in holding it - a distinction examination-format evaluations cannot make. Conclusion: Evaluation in traditional medicine should measure the judgments a consultation requires, not recall alone. Quoted alongside the grader that produced it, a KampoBench score is a usable measure of those judgments.
evidence_items.title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine

organizations: State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, China
evidence_items.summary: Conventional forecasting methods are trained end-to-end on unimodal time series, which limits their ability to exploit textual information and undermines their generalization in data-scarce scenarios. Recently, large language models (LLMs) and time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated powerful capabilities in complex textual reasoning and zero-shot temporal modeling, respectively. Integrating these strengths to construct a multimodal time series foundation model that jointly leverages temporal and textual information for zero-shot future inference has emerged as a promising research direction. However, the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality multimodal datasets remains a fundamental obstacle. To address this challenge, we propose ChronoSteer, a decoupled agentic framework that learns cross-modal alignment from synthetic paired supervision. Specifically, a pretrained LLM first converts textual events into revision instructions that steer the initial unimodal prediction produced by a frozen TSFM. These revision instructions form an intermediate instruction space that bridges the semantic gap between text and time series while fully leveraging pretrained knowledge. Technically, the instructions are discretized into a compact codebook of instruction anchors, effectively mitigating semantic divergence while reducing the cost of dataset construction. Finally, we adopt a two-stage training strategy to recover the fine-grained magnitude information lost during discretization. Furthermore, we release a leakage-controlled multimodal benchmark constructed with temporal separation and textual context available before the prediction window. When paired with an LLM and trained on synthetic cross-modal alignment data, ChronoSteer achieves a 25.8% improvement in zero-shot prediction accuracy over its unimodal backbone, and outperforms prior state-of-the-art unimodal and multimodal methods by 17.8% and 22.5%.
evidence_items.title: ChronoSteer: Bridging Large Language Model and Time Series Foundation Model via Synthetic Cross-Modal Alignment Dataset

organizations: Nanjing Artificial Intelligence Research of IA，Nanjing
The Second Hospital of Jilin University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background This study aimed to develop and externally validate an instruction-tuned multimodal large language model (MLLM) for early warning and early diagnosis of dry eye disease (DED) using routinely obtainable clinical data. Methods A total of 874 participants were enrolled, including an internal development cohort (n = 743) from Peking University Third Hospital (October 2024 to August 2025) and an independent external validation cohort (n = 131) from three additional centers. Participants included both DED and non-DED individuals, diagnosed according to the Chinese Expert Consensus (2020) and TFOS DEWS II criteria. We developed DED-MLLM on the basis of Qwen2-VL and constructed a domain-specific instruction-tuning dataset integrating Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI), Standard Patient Evaluation of Eye Dryness (SPEED), self-reported questionnaires, ophthalmic imaging, and clinical examination data. Model performance was evaluated for risk stratification and diagnosis under both diagnostic frameworks, with ablation analyses used to examine the relative contributions of visual and structured clinical modalities. Results Based on the international diagnostic criteria for DED, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.8232 for early warning (specificity: 0.6873, sensitivity: 0.9558) and an accuracy of 0.9203 for diagnosis (specificity: 0.8776, sensitivity: 0.9720). According to the Chinese diagnostic criteria for DED, the model achieved an accuracy of 0.9584 for early warning (specificity: 0.9112, sensitivity: 0.9927) and an accuracy of 0.9327 for diagnosis (specificity: 0.8742, sensitivity: 0.9851). External validation showed AUCs of 0.910 and 0.957 for early warning and 0.960 and 0.893 for diagnosis. Ablation analyses indicated that structured clinical information contributed most strongly to diagnostic performance, whereas image-based information provided complementary, interpretable ocular-surface evidence.
evidence_items.title: Development of a Multimodal Large Language Model for Early Warning and Diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease

evidence_items.summary: Existing LLM safety benchmarks focus primarily on English and Western contexts, often overlooking the linguistic diversity and culturally grounded safety risks present in other languages. We introduce SurakshaEval, a novel safety benchmark composed of human-written prompts spanning real-world scenarios, explicitly designed for ten major Indian languages - Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Telugu, along with English. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLMs on SurakshaEval, establishing safety baselines and identifying recurring failure modes, including over-refusal and insufficient contextual awareness in regionally sensitive settings, particularly in native scripts. These findings underscore the need for region-specific data and structured evaluations to build safe, ethical, and culturally aligned AI systems. Warning: This paper contains potentially offensive or unsafe content.
evidence_items.title: SurakshaEval: An Indic Safety Benchmark for Multilingual LLMs

College of Law, University of Babylon, Hillah 51002, Babylon, Iraq

evidence_items.summary: Electronic Product Code Information Services (EPCIS) standardizes inter-organizational supply-chain visibility events, yet structurally conformant histories can contain contradictory lifecycle claims that undermine information integrity. We present EPCIS-MutBench, a controlled benchmark and layered validator for evaluating security-relevant semantic and lifecycle integrity in EPCIS 2.0.1 histories. Mutations are treated as integrity violations independently of accidental or adversarial origin; the benchmark evaluates detection and localization rather than attacker attribution. The evaluation uses 2000 deterministic clean histories and 20,000 primary mutants, including 16,000 single-fault and 4000 compound cases, with validator-independent typed ground truth. Across all primary mutants, JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Schema plus compatibility-projected GS1 Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) detected 18.27%, whereas the full event-local and role-aware lifecycle validator detected 95.29%. Among 13,429 single-fault mutants that passed both structural baselines, the full validator achieved 92.98% recall, with end-to-end intended-rule, event, and field/edge localization of 92.90%, 92.19%, and 92.14%, respectively. No false positives occurred on the 2000 generated-clean controls; however, in a separate sensitivity analysis that provisionally treated all 37 parseable external-source fixtures as clean, 19 were marked invalid. A separate attestation layer used cryptographic hashes, Merkle commitments, a digital signature, and public-testnet receipts to make post-freeze evidence modification detectable. The results demonstrate controlled, reproducible evaluation of EPCIS information-integrity assurance beyond structural conformance.
evidence_items.title: EPCIS-MutBench: A Controlled Benchmark for Security-Relevant Semantic and Lifecycle Integrity Validation in EPCIS 2.0.1 Supply-Chain Histories

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are making it easier for the public to interact with government, such as by helping them apply for benefits, understand complex policies, and make their opinions heard. Although improving service accessibility is beneficial, any resulting surges in demand could strain unprepared government services. We term such surges "agentic flooding" of government services (''flooding'') and provide three contributions. First, based on a collected dataset of 84 potential cases of flooding across 11 jurisdictions, we posit that flooding is likely occurring widely today, mostly through large language models (LLMs) generating text cheaply. Second, we evaluate what services are most exposed to flooding. We develop a risk matrix to analyze a service's exposure, and suggest that near-term risk is highest for financially attractive, but complex services. Finally, we map possible government responses to flooding. Precedent suggests these responses will likely be sufficient to stop most cases of flooding, but the fastest to deploy – friction-inducing measures like fees – often trade off equitable access to public services. Accordingly, we close by recommending near-term actions that may allow governments to mitigate flooding without invoking this trade-off.
evidence_items.title: Characterizing Agentic Flooding of Government Services

evidence_items.summary: This study develops a safety-aware supervisory framework for industrial fed-batch bioreactors by integrating an adaptive digital twin, fuzzy multi-objective optimization, Agentic LLM reasoning, and an independent Safety Governor within a closed-loop architecture. The digital twin continuously reconstructs process states and updates sensitive parameters, while α-cut fuzzy intervals preserve biological and operational uncertainty throughout prediction and optimization. The Agentic LLM coordinates prediction, optimization, process knowledge, and candidate evaluation, and supports context-dependent reevaluation and replanning as operating conditions evolve. The framework was evaluated using data from 12 industrial 72 h fed-batch runs, together with 600 uncertainty-aware simulated trajectories. Across three fully independent validation batches, the digital twin achieved an average NRMSE of 4.7%, MAPE of 4.4%, and R2 of 0.985. Closed-loop operation achieved a volumetric productivity of 0.347 g/L·h while maintaining a positive minimum dissolved-oxygen margin of 5 percentage points and zero hard-constraint violations. Across nominal and stressed scenarios, the Safety Governor preserved feasible operation with no residual hard-constraint violations, while the Agentic LLM successfully activated reevaluation and replanning following changes in process conditions. The ablation results further showed that the complete architecture provided the strongest overall balance among productivity, biological risk, robustness, and disturbance recovery. These findings demonstrate the value of combining adaptive process representation, uncertainty-aware optimization, agentic supervisory reasoning, and independent safety validation for reliable intelligent bioprocess operation.
evidence_items.title: A Safety-Aware Agentic LLM–Digital Twin Framework for Fuzzy Multi-Objective Control of Industrial Fed-Batch Bioreactors

evidence_items.summary: Passive reconnaissance has become increasingly significant in helping analysts obtain intelligence about target systems without directly interacting with them. Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT) provides valuable information that can support security assessment, cyber investigation, and forensic analysis. However, information obtained from multiple sources is often redundant, fragmented, and represented in different formats. In this research, an Integrated Passive Reconnaissance and OSINT Correlation Framework is proposed to integrate information gathered from multiple passive intelligence sources, including WHOIS, DNS enumeration, search engine footprinting, and network path analysis. The framework performs information collection, normalization, entity correlation, and consolidation to generate a unified intelligence profile. Through entity correlation across different intelligence sources, the proposed framework reduces redundant information and improves the completeness and consistency of the gathered intelligence. To evaluate the framework, experiments were conducted using publicly available domain-related data. The collected information was processed to assess the framework’s capability to gather, normalize, correlate, and organize intelligence obtained from different OSINT sources. The evaluation used a dataset comprising 1,781 instances and 12 intelligence attributes extracted from multiple reconnaissance sources. The results achieved an attribute availability rate of 90.11% and demonstrated the generation of unified intelligence profiles from the collected reconnaissance information. The findings indicate that integrating heterogeneous passive reconnaissance sources can provide a more complete and structured representation of target intelligence, thereby reducing the manual effort required to consolidate information from multiple sources. The proposed framework provides a foundation for more efficient cyber intelligence gathering and can be extended in future work by incorporating additional OSINT sources and advanced correlation techniques.
evidence_items.title: An integrated passive reconnaissance and OSINT correlation framework for unified cyber intelligence gathering

evidence_items.summary: Cervical artery dissection (CeAD) is a rare but life-threatening condition that commonly presents with non-specific symptoms such as neck and head pain, complicating early recognition in ambulatory care settings. The CeAD diagnostic decision support tool (DDST) is a 4-item assessment designed to identify patients that should be referred for advanced diagnostic work-up to rule out CeAD; however, its utility in ambulatory settings has not been established. This quality improvement project aimed to evaluate the accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability of chiropractors applying the CeAD DDST using clinical vignettes simulating a typical ambulatory encounter before deploying the DDST broadly as part of the clinical workflow. Five experienced chiropractors assessed 40 standardized clinical vignettes. CeAD-positive cases (n = 10) were derived from published imaging-confirmed ambulatory care case reports. CeAD-negative cases (n = 30) were developed using generative artificial intelligence and refined by senior authors to reflect common conditions encountered in chiropractic practice. Raters independently assessed cases with the DDST (score 0–4), with a cutoff score of ≥ 3 recommending referral for advanced diagnostic work-up in two rounds, beginning November 11, 2025 and January 07, 2026, with a two-week capture period. Accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability were assessed. Accuracy in identification ranged from 72.5% to 95.0% across raters and rounds. False positives and negatives were present across raters in both rounds, with false positives being more prevalent. Inter-rater reliability was moderate to substantial in both rounds (Round 1: κ = 0.609, 95% CI 0.432–0.806, Round 2: κ = 0.540, 95% CI 0.365–0.735). Intra-rater reliability ranged from moderate to almost perfect agreement (range 0.457–0.931). The CeAD DDST demonstrated moderate to good accuracy and reliability among chiropractors in a simulated ambulatory setting. The presence of false negatives and inter-rater reliability falling below recommended benchmarks preclude recommendation for implementation at this time. Iterative refinement informed by end-user input and prospective ambulatory testing is warranted prior to clinical adoption of the CeAD DDST. Future evaluations should include prospective studies using real clinical data to better represent real-world settings.
evidence_items.title: Preliminary accuracy, inter- and intra-rater reliability of a 4-point cervical artery dissection diagnostic decision support tool in an ambulatory setting using real and simulated cases: a quality improvement project

evidence_items.summary: Authentic assessment seeks to evaluate students through work resembling professional practice, but complex professional tasks can exceed the procedural capabilities of undergraduate novices. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) may alter this constraint by providing on-demand procedural support while leaving judgment-dependent dimensions of performance available for assessment. This single-semester case study examines an AI-integrated undergraduate qualitative research methods course in which students were expected to use AI throughout development of a publishable research manuscript. The quantitative corpus comprised 33 final manuscripts produced under unrestricted AI access. Three rule-based, rubric-proximal indicators were used to estimate dispersion. The Methods Specificity Index showed strong upper-bound compression: the median was 6 on a 0–6 scale, 69.7% of manuscripts received the maximum score, and 97.0% scored either 5 or 6. Claim–Evidence Coupling remained substantially dispersed (range = 0.000–0.750, median = 0.333, Q1–Q3 = 0.273–0.542, IQR = 0.269), as did Theory–Interpretation Linkage (range = 0.000–0.917, median = 0.444, Q1–Q3 = 0.250–0.500, IQR = 0.250). Qualitative comparison of four contrasting student cases identified three recurring process differences associated with stronger outcomes: criteria-based orchestration, provision of irreducible project-specific inputs, and substantive multi-turn iteration. In this course, unrestricted AI access therefore did not eliminate meaningful variation in student products. Structural aspects of research writing clustered near competence, while dimensions requiring evidence integration and theoretical judgment remained diagnostic. The case suggests that authentic assessment can remain viable in AI-integrated undergraduate settings when assessment design distinguishes between work AI can scaffold reliably and forms of judgment students must still exercise.
evidence_items.title: Authentic assessment in an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course

evidence_items.summary: Conventional in-situ monitoring solutions—such as high-speed cameras, SWIR imaging, and acoustic emission sensors—are costly, data-intensive, and impractical for industrial deployment. In this work, we demonstrate a low-cost, off-the-shelf ultrasonic microphone installed inside the build chamber as a practical alternative for capturing high-resolution acoustic signals during LPBF. Using these signals, we benchmark multiple machine learning architectures for localized porosity prediction. Targets for lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity are derived from volumetric X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT) analysis and carefully registered to process coordinates, enabling supervised learning at scanline granularity. Beyond performance evaluation, we conduct explainability analysis using feature attribution methods to uncover which acoustic signatures most strongly correlate with defect formation. Results show that acoustic-based models achieve low-latency inference, suitable for in-process monitoring, paving the way for adaptive corrective control strategies. This study establishes a new paradigm for practical, scalable LPBF quality assurance by combining low-cost sensing with interpretable AI.
evidence_items.title: Sound Of Porosity: Unlocking Local Acoustic Signatures Of Porosity In LPBF Via Low-Cost Sensing And Explainable AI

evidence_items.summary: Bovine coronavirus (BCoV), a primary etiological agent of calf diarrhea, exhibits dual tropism for the respiratory and enteric tracts. However, research on BCoV gene function and pathogenesis has been limited by the lack of convenient and flexible reverse genetics tools. Herein, we report a robust reverse genetics system for BCoV based on an optimized circular polymerase extension reaction (CPER) methodology. We successfully rescued recombinant BCoV (rBCoV) in HRT-18G cells and engineered recombinant BCoV expressing ZsGreen fluorescent protein (rBCoV/Zs-T2A-ns2). Phenotypic analysis demonstrated that both unmodified rBCoV and rBCoV/Zs-T2A-ns2 maintained growth kinetics comparable to the wild-type BCoV. Importantly, the reporter virus demonstrated remarkable genetic stability for over ten passages, identifying the ns2 locus as a suitable insertion site for stable foreign gene expression without compromising viral fitness or sequence integrity. As a proof-of-concept application, the rBCoV/Zs-T2A-ns2 was employed for antiviral compound evaluation, successfully identifying four compounds—camostat, nafamostat, niclosamide, and nelfinavir—capable of effectively inhibiting BCoV replication. Further time-of-addition assays revealed that nelfinavir and niclosamide targeted the BCoV replication stage, while camostat and nafamostat interfered with BCoV internalization. This versatile CPER-based reverse genetics system provides a critical platform for advanced BCoV pathogenesis research and accelerated development of novel vaccines and effective antiviral therapeutics, ultimately contributing to enhanced bovine health and sustainable livestock production.
evidence_items.title: An efficient and versatile reverse genetics system for bovine coronavirus facilitates antiviral evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Background. Classical macroparasite models commonly represent worm burden heterogeneity through prescribed Poisson or negative-binomial (NB) distributions, while transmission dynamics are formulated in terms of aggregate quantities such as mean worm burden and prevalence. We revisit these assumptions using a stratified worm burden (SWB) framework that explicitly tracks the distribution of parasite burdens across heterogeneous host classes and allows demographic turnover, transmission, and interventions to be analyzed within a unified model. Methods. We derive equilibrium distributions of the SWB system under homogeneous and heterogeneous infection processes and compare them with the classical Poisson and NB distributions used in macroparasite epidemiology and control policymaking. The framework is then extended to include host demography, coupled human-snail transmission dynamics, and periodic mass drug administration (MDA). Corresponding SWB and NB-type MacDonald models are calibrated to comparable endemic prevalence and mean worm burden, allowing direct comparison of potential transmission breakpoints and intervention outcomes. Results. In the absence of demographic turnover, the SWB framework naturally generates Poisson and NB equilibrium distributions as limiting cases of homogeneous and heterogeneous infection processes. Incorporating demographic recruitment and mortality alters these benchmark distributions, producing endemic burden structures that differ systematically from their classical counterparts. Analysis of coupled human-snail systems reveals that transmission breakpoints and bistable equilibria occur only within a relatively restricted region of SWB parameter space. In contrast, comparable NB-MacDonald formulations exhibit breakpoint behavior over substantially broader parameter ranges with the net effect of overestimating the likelihood of interruption of transmission. Although calibrated models can reproduce near identical endemic prevalence and mean worm burden, they often generate markedly different responses to MDA, including differences in rebound dynamics, persistence, and elimination thresholds. Conclusions. The SWB framework links classical statistical descriptions of worm aggregation to mechanistic burden-resolved population dynamics, clarifying how endemic distributions emerge and how they are modified by demography and control interventions. Our results suggest that transmission breakpoints are not a universal feature of helminth systems but depend strongly on model structure, and that predictions of elimination and post-treatment recovery may be considerably more model-dependent than implied by prevalence-based calibration alone. The SWB approach therefore provides a flexible alternative framework for evaluating parasite transmission dynamics and predicting the outcomes of control strategies.
evidence_items.title: A Stratified Worm Burden Framework for Endemic Equilibria, Demography, and Mass Drug Administration: Linking Classical Macroparasite Models to Transmission Dynamics

evidence_items.summary: ImpactAlign SDG is a proposed conceptual framework designed to help organizations understand, plan, assess, and communicate how their projects, programmes, policies, and initiatives contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Although many development activities aim to support sustainable development, their connections with specific SDG goals, targets, and indicators are not always clearly defined or supported by measurable evidence. ImpactAlign SDG seeks to address this challenge by providing a structured approach to identifying SDG alignment and assessing development-related results. The framework connects project objectives and activities with relevant SDG goals, targets, and indicators. It follows a logical results pathway from inputs and activities to outputs, outcomes, and longer-term impacts. Through this approach, organizations can examine what they plan to achieve, what results they actually produce, and how those results relate to wider sustainable development priorities. The framework also encourages the use of reliable data, clear performance measures, stakeholder participation, and appropriate monitoring and evaluation methods. A key feature of ImpactAlign SDG is its focus on the quality and credibility of SDG alignment. Rather than assuming that a project contributes to an SDG simply because it addresses a related issue, the framework encourages organizations to explain the connection using clear objectives, relevant indicators, and supporting evidence. It also considers potential trade-offs between development priorities, cross-cutting sustainability issues, and the possibility that a project may contribute to several SDGs at the same time. Importantly, it distinguishes between activities that are aligned with an SDG, results that demonstrate progress, and impacts that can be reasonably linked to an intervention.
evidence_items.title: ImpactAlign SDG: A Conceptual Framework for  Sustainable Development Goal Alignment and Impact  Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Safety evaluations of large language models (LLMs) are typically conducted using full-precision reference weights under exact autoregressive decoding, despite production systems commonly deploying quantized models, evicted or quantized key–value (KV) caches, and speculative decoding. Recent audits show meaningful safety degradation from weight and cache compression individually, but the safety impact of deployed, non-exact speculative decoding and the interaction among multiple transformations remain poorly understood. We address two open questions. First, we examine non-preserving speculative decoding variants, including typical acceptance, entropy-adjusted thresholds, tree-structured drafting, and n-gram paths verified by argmax match. Second, we investigate whether composing weight compression, KV-cache compression, and speculative decoding produces sub-additive or super-additive safety degradation. Across five production serving frameworks, we find that although most default to exact rejection sampling, all expose non-preserving alternatives, with practitioner guidance recommending their use for quantized target models which is a potentially high-risk combination. We formalize acceptance relaxation and decompose its distributional shift into two opposing channels, a mode-seeking term that sharpens toward the target model’s distribution and may be safety-protective, and a draft-leakage term that substitutes the draft model’s distribution for the target’s and represents the primary hazard. GPU-free Monte Carlo experiments validate this decomposition and show that exact rejection sampling remains at the noise floor, whereas typical acceptance and argmax-match reach 25× and 12× the noise level, respectively. We further falsify our initial hypothesis of a positive relaxation-by-alignment interaction, obtaining a coefficient of − 1.23 (R² = 0.92).
evidence_items.title: Speculative Decoding Shortcuts Can Undermine Language Model Safety Guarantees

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Text embedding models are routinely compared using a single aggregate score on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB), yet an aggregate conceals whether a model performs uniformly across task families or excels narrowly on a subset of them. We revisit the original MTEB English-subset results (30 models, 7 task categories) and ask a question the original benchmark report did not directly quantify: is high aggregate performance associated with high cross-task consistency, and does model scale buy consistency in the same way it buys average performance? Using the publicly released per-model, per-task scores, we compute pairwise task correlations, a z-score-based cross-task profile dispersion index for every model, and a Ward hierarchical clustering of models by task profile. We find that profile dispersion is negatively associated with average score (Pearson r = − 0.48, p = 0.008), indicating that top-performing models tend to be more uniformly competent rather than narrowly optimized, but dispersion is essentially uncorrelated with parameter count (r = − 0.003, p = 0.99), indicating that scale alone does not confer cross-task balance. Clustering recovers four qualitatively distinct groups, including a "retrieval-and-reranking specialist" cluster with a pronounced summarization deficit and a fifteen-model "balanced generalist" cluster spanning multiple architectures. These findings reframe model-selection guidance for practitioners and motivate reporting dispersion alongside average score in future embedding leaderboards. All data, code and derived tables are made available for reproducibility [1].
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Leaderboard Average: Cross-Task Consistency, Model Scale, and Specialization Structure in the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Background Inadequate or misleading health information about silicosis can delay diagnosis, reporting, and exposure removal, potentially affecting risk communication and timely occupational health interventions. Objective This study evaluates the reliability, quality, and readability of Large Language Models (LLMs) including ChatGPT (GPT-5), Gemini (2.5 Flash), and Copilot (Smart GPT-5), in answering patient-oriented silicosis questions, focusing on risk communication rather than clinical decisions. Methods Silicosis-related questions were collected from online forums (September 1–7, 2025), and 25 frequently asked, clinically relevant questions were selected and submitted to the LLMs (September 8–14, 2025). Two occupational medicine specialists/pulmonologists independently evaluated responses (September 15–30, 2025) for reliability, quality, and readability using modified DISCERN, Global Quality Scale, and readability indices. Analyses used SPSS version 31.0. Results The LLM-generated responses demonstrated fair reliability. Median (min–max) scores were 23 (12–27) for ChatGPT, 21.5 (14–29) for Gemini, and 26 (17.5–31) for Copilot. Copilot scored significantly higher than ChatGPT and Gemini (p = 0.014). GQS scores were similar across models (p = 0.102), with median scores of 4 (3–5) for ChatGPT and Copilot and 4 (2–5) for Gemini. Readability levels corresponded predominantly to secondary or tertiary education, with no significant differences between the models (all p > 0.05). Conclusion LLMs may enhance worker awareness but have limitations in accuracy and readability. They should complement, not replace, expert-supervised occupational health services. Future studies should align LLMs with international standards, improve accessibility, and establish governance frameworks for transparent and equitable AI use in occupational health.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of the reliability, quality, and readability of multiple large language model responses (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot) on silicosis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models are increasingly used in healthcare. Nursing students need to strengthen academic writing with such technologies, but existing qualitative evidence is fragmented. To synthesize qualitative evidence on nursing students' experiences using large language models for academic writing to inform future education. Methods PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang Data, VIP Database, and SinoMed were searched for relevant qualitative studies from database inception to January 22, 2026. The JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research was used to evaluate study quality, and findings were synthesized using the JBI meta-aggregation approach. Results A total of 11 studies were included. Thirty-nine findings were extracted, grouped into 13 categories, and further synthesized into 5 synthesized findings: perceived usefulness; perceived ease of use and usage practices; perceived risks and limitations; external factors; and the formation of behavioral intention. Conclusion Nursing students generally hold positive attitudes toward using large language models for academic writing, while expressing concerns about content quality and ethical risks. Future efforts should include systematic training and standardized usage guidelines, as well as measures to emphasize the irreplaceable role of humanistic care and clinical judgment in nursing.
evidence_items.title: Nursing Students' Experiences with Large Language Models in Academic Writing: A Qualitative Systematic Review Based on the Technology Acceptance Model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) systems, especially large language models (LLMs), face growing constraints related to energy use, power delivery, memory traffic, experimentation, and infrastructure capacity. These pressures are often studied separately, which makes it difficult to understand how they interact across the full AI lifecycle. This review develops a cross-layer framework that brings these constraints together and examines whether resource-allocation strategies observed in human cognition can inform more sustainable AI design. We compare human and artificial systems by function rather than anatomy, focusing on how each allocates limited resources to learning, search, memory, external support, optimization, and inference. Using a systematized narrative-review approach, we identified 6284 records, screened 898 at the full-text stage, and selected an initial set of 150 focal studies for detailed synthesis. We organize the evidence into seven interacting regimes covering scaling, experimentation, hardware power limits, data movement, infrastructure, evaluation incentives, and inference allocation. The framework extends Green AI by linking these layers and translating insights from human cognition into testable design hypotheses and measurable evaluation criteria. The strongest near-term opportunities include data selection, energy-aware experimentation, hardware-supported low-precision computation, and demand-adaptive inference. However, most reported gains are based on proxy measures such as operations, memory, latency, or data volume rather than direct end-to-end energy measurements. Near- and in-memory computing show longer-term promise, while retrieval, tool use, distributed experts, and multi-agent systems may shift or increase energy costs through communication and repeated inference. These findings support cross-layer co-design and end-to-end evaluation at matched capability, reliability, latency, and service quality.
evidence_items.title: Energy constraints in large scale artificial intelligence and insights from human cognition for efficient large language models

organizations: School of Foreign Languages, Northeast Normal University, Changchun, China
evidence_items.summary: This study examines translation style variation across registers in English Chinese outputs from TencentMT, DeepSeek, and ArkLLM. Using an aligned corpus of public speech, legal-diplomatic texts, and news, it compares length ratio, mean sentence length, and connective density through mixed-effects modelling and qualitative analysis. ArkLLM generally produced longer outputs, while TencentMT produced shorter sentences and used more explicit connectives. Register also shaped these patterns, showing that AI translation style varies across systems and communicative contexts.
evidence_items.title:

evidence_items.summary: Abstract RNA therapeutics are increasingly moving from empirical screening towards rational, computation‐guided design. Recent advances in RNA language models, generative models and structure‐aware learning have improved sequence representation, candidate generation and structure‐constrained optimization. However, favourable molecular properties do not necessarily translate into desirable biological performance, because therapeutic outcomes also depend on modality‐specific mechanisms, delivery and exposure, molecular interactions, cellular state, immune responses and network‐level adaptation. Here, we review AI‐enabled RNA therapeutic design through the specific lens of the interface between molecular optimization and system‐level evaluation. We compare the design constraints of siRNAs, antisense oligonucleotides, aptamers, mRNAs and translation‐oriented circRNAs, and examine the capabilities and current limitations of sequence‐, generative‐ and structure‐based computational models. We further discuss the data resources and perturbation representations required to connect molecular candidates with broader cellular‐response models. In this context, virtual cells are considered as approximate computational frameworks for candidate prioritization and risk‐oriented system‐level assessment rather than complete digital replicas of living cells. Finally, we outline a conceptual generation–simulation–feedback–optimization framework for integrating molecular design with progressively higher‐level evaluation. This perspective emphasizes the need for better interfaces among RNA design, pharmacological context and cellular‐response modelling, rather than relying on molecular optimization alone.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI)‐enabled RNA therapeutic design: from molecular optimization to system‐level evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Bile duct hyperplasia in rodents, caused by chemical cytotoxicity, bile flow interference, or aging, is traditionally assessed through time-consuming microscopic examination by pathologists. We developed a deep learning-based, artificial intelligence (AI) model for quick and accurate assessment of bile duct hyperplasia in mice. The study utilized 127 hematoxylin and eosin-stained, mouse liver whole-slide images (WSIs) digitized using Aperio scanners. A segmentation algorithm with a U-Net architecture and an EfficientNet backbone was trained on 1165 areas from 35 WSIs to identify and quantify bile ducts, measure their area percentage using a supervised method, and categorize them into grades 0 to 4 using an unsupervised method. The model was validated on 24 WSIs and tested on 68 WSIs, all independently scored by 3 veterinary pathologists using consensus criteria. The segmentation model achieved Dice scores of 91.75% in training and 85.88% in validation. Testing revealed high sensitivity (95%), specificity (97%), and Dice score (95.45%), indicating robust model accuracy. Model-predicted grades showed strong correlation ( r 2 s = 0.86) with pathologists’ consensus scores. This AI-driven approach has the potential to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of bile duct hyperplasia assessments in rodent studies, paving the way for more standardized, objective, and high-throughput histological evaluations in preclinical research.
evidence_items.title: Comparative evaluation of artificial intelligence-based and pathologist scoring of murine bile duct hyperplasia

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on buyer–supplier relationship quality in Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, with specific reference to TECNO Mobile Nigeria. Drawing on the Commitment-Trust Theory of Relationship Marketing (Morgan & Hunt, 1994), the study operationalises AI through three proxies: Predictive Analytics (PA), Automation of Processes (AP), and AI Risk Management (AIR). A survey research design was adopted, and structured questionnaires were administered to 250 employees and supply chain partners purposively selected from TECNO Mobile's procurement, logistics, IT, and supplier management functions. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (frequencies, means, standard deviations) and one-sample t-tests benchmarked against the scale's neutral midpoint (μ₀ = 3.00). All three null hypotheses were rejected at p < 0.001. Predictive Analytics recorded an aggregate mean of 3.88 (SD = 0.34; t(249) = 40.53), Automation of Processes 3.91 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.05), and AI Risk Management 3.92 (SD = 0.36; t(249) = 40.47), all significantly above the neutral midpoint. Findings confirm that respondents perceive each AI dimension as positively and meaningfully contributing to trust, efficiency, transparency, and long-term relational stability with suppliers. The study contributes empirical evidence from an under-studied domain in the AI-supply chain literature, Nigeria's mobile manufacturing sector, and offers practical guidance for practitioners and policymakers pursuing AI-enabled supply chain transformation in emerging economies.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Buyer–Supplier Relationships in Procurement

organizations: Universidad de Ciencias Médicas de Villa Clara, Facultad de Medicina. Santa Clara, Cuba.
evidence_items.summary: Introduction: artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how diseases are diagnosed, treated and monitored, integrating machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing into the analysis of large volumes of clinical data. Objective: to comprehensively analyze the impact of artificial intelligence on medicine, examining its main diagnostic, therapeutic and clinical-management applications, as well as the challenges, limitations and ethical considerations that condition its safe, equitable and patient-centered integration. Development: AI has matured most in medical imaging, oncology and precision medicine, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgment; randomized evidence in cardiology shows improved workflow efficiency and reduced adverse events, including all-cause mortality. Implementation nonetheless faces technical, organizational and social barriers—data quality and interoperability, lack of explainability, algorithmic bias, and gaps in clinician training—alongside ethical and regulatory challenges regarding privacy, accountability and informed consent. Conclusions: AI offers considerable potential to reduce costs, increase diagnostic accuracy, personalize care and expand access to quality services, provided its deployment overcomes technical, ethical and regulatory barriers through proactive, adaptive and patient-centered governance.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: diagnostic, therapeutic and ethical impact

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Trust in new technologies is often seen as a key condition for their implementation in everyday life, as the aim is for users to utilise technical innovations without strong reservations. The aspect of trust also plays a fundamental role in the discourse on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its far-reaching consequences for people’s lives. In this context, journalistic reporting as part of the public discourse plays a considerable role in creating trust or distrust in AI as a new technology. Whether and how trust issues are addressed in journalistic reporting has not been investigated so far. The paper explores how AI is depicted in German journalistic coverage, covering the topics of autonomous driving and smart home systems, which we expected to generate diverging trust issues. Furthermore, we show how trustworthiness and untrustworthiness are constructed in those texts, choosing AI applications intended for everyday use and therefore relying on trust from users ( Tschopp et al. 2022 ; Gillespie et al. 2021 ). We carried out a qualitative linguistic content analysis on a corpus of German press texts from 2023 that are dedicated to the aforementioned topics. We focused our analysis on explicit and implicit trust communication in the journalistic coverage of AI and examined whether qualitative differences can be identified in the way trust or distrust is addressed in various sub-discourses.
evidence_items.title: Addressing trust and distrust in artificial intelligence in newspaper texts

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) holds considerable promise for improving cardiovascular care, but prior to widespread adoption AI-powered tools require evaluation in randomised trials. We systematically reviewed the current evidence from randomised trials of AI tools in cardiovascular medicine. Methods We conducted a systematic review of randomised trials comparing AI tools vs. standard care in cardiovascular medicine. PubMed, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform were searched from January 1, 2018, to April 10, 2026. Screening and full-text review were performed by three independent reviewers and risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2 criteria. Results Of 11,151 identified records, 8,599 remained after removal of duplicates. Following screening and full-text review, 25 trials met the eligibility criteria. These trials evaluated AI tools in acute cardiovascular care (n = 3), cardiac imaging (n = 6), decision support for medical therapy (n = 6), electrophysiology (n = 8), and interventional cardiology (n = 2). Nine trials were single-centre, and two were international. Seventeen trials (68%) reported positive results, defined by non-inferiority or superiority of the AI-based strategy. Overall risk of bias was rated as high or with some concerns in 84% of the included trials, and only 36% explicitly reported following the CONSORT-/SPIRIT-AI reporting guidelines. Discussion Evidence from randomised trials evaluating AI tools in cardiovascular medicine is limited and most trials have a high risk of bias. Wider implementation of AI tools into practice requires robust, international, multi-centre randomised trials that evaluate patient-relevant outcomes, ensure external validity, and adhere to reporting guidelines. Trial registration number: PROSPERO CRD420251019264
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular medicine: systematic review of randomised controlled trials

organizations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics
evidence_items.summary: Abstract We study the flavor structure of Majorana neutrino masses in a modular messenger realization of lepton-number-violating $R$-parity violation. Homogeneous level-three modular symmetry, with $\Gamma' 3\simeq T'$ and an even-weight sector descending to $A 4$, relates bilinear and third-family lepton--quark couplings at a common modulus. Renormalizable mediator chains generate these interactions, and baryon triality forbids the baryon-number-violating operator. The charged-lepton and soft-sector alignments define the benchmark. The retained neutrino mass texture contains neutralino-tree and bottom--sbottom rank-one contributions and leaves one neutrino massless. For a weight-four loop direction, a bilinear displacement within the weight-two and weight-four plane preserves the massless mixing column. A symmetric weight-six loop contribution allows both deformations to change that column. The extended textures accommodate both neutrino mass orderings. Four $501\times501$ modulus profiles determine their oscillation-compatible regions and associated mass and flavor observables. Representative solutions give $m {\beta\beta}$ between $1.47$ and $3.75$ meV for normal ordering and between $17.8$ and $48.2$ meV for inverted ordering, within the kinematic envelope of a massless neutrino spectrum. The mass sum and beta-decay mass-parameter provide complementary ordering signatures. We connect the fitted flavor coefficients to weak-scale neutralino and sbottom contributions by inverse matching and derive a conditional charged-current neutralino-decay flavor correlation.
evidence_items.title: A modular messenger benchmark for rank-two neutrino masses in lepton-number-violating R-parity violation

organizations: Department of Civil Engineering, SVKM NMIMS Global University, Dhule 424001, Maharashtra, India
